“The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

The range and scope of short stories are exactly the same as those of plays, but short-story writers must know the technique of presenting a long story concisely. Suspense is equally effective in short stories as in plays; dramatic skill is essential for the writer of those short stories which come in the category of sketches, because a sketch holds an intermediate position between a story and a play. ”

In the unique and superb interpretation of sáhitya, literature, in terms of ‘Art for service and blessedness,’ given above, the author has provided eternal guidance to all those related to the world of literature. With the basic objectives set by the author, literature with all its branches, including plays and short stories, can truly build up an ideal and just society, which is the demand of the day.

Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar (also known as Shrii Shrii Ánandamúrti, a spiritual Guru) elaborately explained his views on art and literature in the discourse (“Art and Literature”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1) quoted above. But he did not stop there. Going a step further, he translated his words into actions, giving a direct example by creating his own literature, which is marked by his natural ease and aptitude. Thus a great series named Sarkarʼs Short Stories was written in fourteen parts. In June 1985, the first Bengali fourteen-part series was published under the authorʼs direct guidance. In January 1990, the English Sarkarʼs Short Stories Part 1 was published. Since then, there has been a persistent demand from our esteemed readers for the publication of all the parts. In response to that, in October 2010, a volume named Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 1-3 in one volume was published. Now, we are extremely happy to publish Sarkarʼs Short Stories Parts 4, 5, 6. Genuine and sincere efforts are going on to publish all the remaining parts within the next year. We fervently hope to fulfil this objective with the cooperation of all concerned.

All stories belonging to the Sarkarʼs Short Stories series appeared originally as important and integral parts of the authorʼs writings on a vast range of topics from linguistics and philology to history, geography, medicine, science, art, religion, spirituality, philosophy, etc. Such books included Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá (eight parts) and Shabda Cayaniká (twenty-six parts). Like most great authors, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar is a consummate storyteller, thus he used in those books a seemingly inexhaustible supply of anecdotes, personal experiences and interesting as well as educative references, in order to capture the readerʼs interest. And it is mostly those stories that have been excerpted to constitute the present book. Thus it is natural that in the stories contained in the present book, we will find, either at the beginnings of those stories or as footnotes, relevant references to the linguistic and other subjects of the original books. In this way the stories retain the authenticity of the original books.

In the present volume, Part 4 contains seventeen stories from Varńa Vicitrá Parts 7 and 8 which are translated from the original Bengali as the above-named books were not printed in English. Part 5 contains eight stories from Varńa Vicitrá Part 8 which are also translated in the present volume. The last two stories (ten stories in all) are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1, which is available in English, but properly re-edited. Part 6 contains eight long stories from Shabda Cayaniká Part 1 and 2 also properly re-edited. At the end of this note the “Sources” for each story are included.

It is interesting to note that the two last two stories in Part 5 and all the stories in Part 6 describe the authorʼs personal para psychological experiences. They take the reader on a journey into the little known world of “Dream and Reality”, evoking deep feelings of pathos. At the beginning of each such story the author sets the scene in a way that will help the reader to understand the inner spirit of the stories.

In this respect it will be useful to quote the following: “Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence. Anyhow, all this happens in the flow of consciousness, sometimes in a very natural, and sometimes in an unnatural rhythmic flow. This was consciousness or its negative, unconsciousness.”
In the interest of accuracy, the authorʼs explanations of certain Sanskrit, Bengali and other terminologies have all been retained in full.
Source references for all the material in the book are provided at the end of this publisherʼs note.
Footnotes by the translators have all been signed “–Trans.” Unsigned footnotes are those of the author.

Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs published discourses, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise words the author used while speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words.
As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. 'Man is mortalʼ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

The author was a natural advocate of womenʼs rights and on at least one occasion indicated that “lopsided justice” in language should be eliminated at some future date. In keeping with his guidelines and with current trends, it is our policy in the case of translated discourses (where the published wording will necessarily be that of the translators) to use gender-neutral language.

Square brackets [ ] in the text are used to indicate translations by the editors or other editorial insertions. Round brackets ( ) indicate a word or words originally used by the author. When round brackets follow an English word or phrase and contain the equivalent Bengali word or phrase, it should be understood that the English words represent the English translation, while the contents of the brackets are the original Bengali words provided as extra information for the reader.

The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. Thus ava – tr + ghaiṋ = avatára can be read, “the root tr prefixed by ava and suffixed by ghaiṋ becomes avatára.”

The verbal root bat́ means to grow, to acquire strength, to exhibit strength. In common parlance, the ba that we get by adding d́a to the verbal root bat́ means “one that gathers strength or displays strength”. The banyan tree does not stop growing. So one meaning of ba (bat́ + d́a) is banyan tree. Bat́ > bad́a > baŕa.

In Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, a banyan tree is colloquially referred to as bar. In Persian and Urdu it is called bargad. The banyan tree belongs to the family of trees which does not stop growing; it keeps on growing. There are many species ( 1 ) of banyan tree in the world; among them, the Chinese and Indian species are the most noteworthy. The Indian banyan tree (Banian indica) grows aerial roots ( 2 ) from its main trunk rather quickly. These aerial roots later grow into trunks. Some banyan trees have a large number of trunks. Sometimes it happens that even after the original trunk has been eaten up by white ants ( 3 ) [termites] or caterpillars, the tree survives and remains in good health due to its well-developed aerial roots. The banyan tree in the botanical garden of Kolkata and the banyan tree standing in the vicinity of Bagchi-Jamshedpur in Nadia District are estimated to be more than four thousand years old. In fact, the second one may be even older. Many people say that the banyan tree obtained its unending longevity as a boon from Sita. Let me briefly tell you that [mythological] story.

At the time of this story, Rama and Laksman were living in the forest. They had to travel to Gaya, situated on the bank of the river Phalgu. This river was formed from the union of rivers Nairanjana and Mohaniya, both originating from the south. At the time of the obsequies of Dasarath [father of Rama and Laksmana], Rama, Laksmana and Sita were staying on the bank of the Phalgu. However, the obsequies were delayed.

Sita was sitting alone on the bank of the Phalgu as Rama and Laksmana had gone to Gaya ( 4 ) to collect materials and arrange for the shráddha [funeral rites] ceremony and probably also to visit the barber to shave their heads [as per Hindu funerary custom]. Suddenly, Sita noticed that a spirit was standing before her with outstretched hand, saying, “Pińd́aḿ dehi” [Give me my oblation please].
Sita asked the spirit, “Who are you?”
The spirit answered, “I am your father-in-law.”
Sita said, “Your sons have gone shopping ( 5 ) downtown. They will offer you oblation on their return.”

The spirit of Dasarath disappeared. After some time, the spirit reappeared and said to Sita again, “Pińd́aḿ dehi”. Sita repeated what she had said before. The spirit said, “I canʼt wait any longer. Please dedicate something to the Phalgu in my name.”
Sita said, “It is not customary to receive oblation from the daughter-in-law when your son is alive. Please wait a little longer.”
The spirit replied, “I am not able to wait anymore.”

According to social customs, one should not perform ceremonies like marriage, obsequies and rice-eating ceremony [rice-eating ceremony means annapráshan in Bengali] secretly. They should be performed publicly for societal approbation. But, when Sita saw that the spirit of Dasarath had grown so impatient, she took a handful of sand and threw it in the Phalgu in the name of Dasarath as his oblation. The spirit of Dasarath disappeared.

After some time, Rama and Lakshmana completed their shopping and arrived with a porter carrying a huge load on his head. When they saw Sita sitting on the bank of the Phalgu with a vacant look, they asked her, “Whatʼs the matter? Why are you sitting here like this?”
Sita said, “Just now, I offered oblation to my father-in-law with a handful of sand. Your shopping has been in vain.”
Both Rama and Lakshmana replied, “While offering oblation, one has to have a witness. Who saw you offering oblation?”
Sita replied, “It was witnessed by the river Phalgu, that basil plant nearby, that keyá [screwpine] plant and that huge banyan tree.”
Rama and Lakshman said to Sita, “You ask them. If they say ‘yes’, we will accept your oblation.”
Sita asked the Phalgu, “Phalgu, I have thrown the oblation into your waters. Please tell the truth.”

The Phalgu thought: “Rama and Lakshman have practically bought the entire market for the oblation ceremony; if I now say that Sita has already offered the oblation with sand, they will certainly feel hurt.” So, to please Rama, the river just kept mum instead of telling the truth.

Sita said. “Phalgu, donʼt you know that hiding the truth is a worse crime than lying? I put a curse on you! From now on, you will flow under the ground. This means that sand will be on top and you will flow under the sand. To collect water from the Phalgu, one will have to dig the sand!”

Sita then turned to the basil plant, “Tell me whether you saw me offering oblation in sand to my deceased father-in-law. Please tell the truth. You are used in different kinds of worship – your leaves are used to worship Hari, people make necklaces from your twigs. That is why your name is Haripriyá. According to mythology, you are the wife of Ganapati. I expect you to tell the truth.”

But the basil also remained silent to please Rama and Laksmana. Sita felt annoyed and said, “Basil, you have abused your position. It is good not to use oneʼs position, but to abuse it is not good at all; it does more harm to people. I curse you! Lowly animals will urinate on your body when they pass by you!”

Sita then asked ketakii [screwpine flower], “Ketakii, you are admired for your fragrance. You are famous in all the three worlds. Your fame is well established. In the rainy season, you float about in the sky, air and distant horizon along with the wind, drenched with water particles. I expect you to be truthful.”

But, the ketakii also remained silent to please Rama and Laksmana. Sita said, “Must one lose oneʼs integrity like this once one has an established reputation? I curse you! From today onwards, you will be considered unfit for use in the worship of the divinities!” Since then, the use of ketakii had been proscribed in the worship of the divinities.

Finally, Sita turned to the banyan tree. “You, banyan tree, you are truly a great tree. You provide safe shelter for hundreds of birds and insects. You tell me, in keeping with your majesty and magnanimity, whether I have offered oblation of sand to my father-in-law.”

The banyan tree said, “I donʼt care for anybody in this vast universe. I love the Supreme Being but I am not afraid of Him. The Supreme Being is always with me. Why should I be afraid of Him? It does not matter to me whether Rama is delighted or saddened. The fact is that I saw Sita offering sand as oblation in the name of her father-in-law.”

Rama and Laksmana accepted the evidence of the banyan tree. Sita said, “I bless you – may you have unending longevity. The aerial roots that descend from you will grow into new and newer trunks. Your life will flow on and on, century after century.”
Since then, the banyan tree has been known as the undecaying banyan tree.

The verbal root bal means “to live”, “to gather strength”. By adding the suffix nini to the verbal root bal we get the word Balii, the etymological meaning of which is ‘one who has strength.’ In common parlance, the word refers to MahaBalii, the king of demons, who is famous in mythology for his charity. Anything excessive is condemnable. It is said:
Atidarpe ( 1 ) hatá lauṋká, ati máne ca kaoraváh,
Ati dáne Baliirbaddhah ati sarvatra varjayet.

[Lanka was destroyed due to excessive pride [of Ravana]; the Kaoravas were destroyed due to excessive vanity; Balii had to die due to his excessive charity. So anything excessive should always be avoided.]

Yes, this King Balii was puffed up with pride over his charitable disposition. According to mythology, Náráyańa appeared before him in the form of a dwarf and asked for a piece of land big enough to put three feet on.
As the story goes, King Balii at once said, “How much land can a dwarf need for putting three feet! I am giving it to you right now.”

Náráyańa then assumed a huge form and put one foot on the earth. The whole earth was covered by that foot. He raised the second foot towards heaven and that covered the entire heaven. Then he asked Balii, “Where should I put my third foot?”

Balii was bound by his promise to give him land for three feet. As there was no other alternative, he said, “Please put your third foot on my head.” Náráyańa placed the third foot on the head of Balii, and the weight of that foot sent Balii to hell.

Although it is just a myth, it imparts the lesson that one should not be proud of anything, because whatever earthly thing we are proud of is perishable (nash + barac = nashvar, which means perishable). If one has to take pride in anything, one should take pride in what is imperishable or indestructible. The latter can only be found in Parama Puruśa. That is why a Vaeśńava [follower of Viśńu] poet said through the character of Shrii Radha:
Baṋdhu tamári garave garavinii ámi
Rupasii tomári rúpe.
[My dear, I am proud in your pride
I am beautiful in your beauty.]

The son of King Balii was King Báńa. King Báńa was a devotee of Lord Shiva. Báńeshvar, one of the names of Lord Shiva, is derived from the name of King Báńa. The historical King Báńa was possibly a king of some part of Bengal. There are certain places in Bengal which are named after him; for example, Báńaeshvar and Báńagaŕ. In common parlance, one of the meanings of the word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is Balii, the demon King. It is this King Balii who is better known as MahaBalii. King Balii, who is still highly regarded in the most remote parts of Kerala in South India, is invariably associated with the name of Viśńu or Náráyańa. Náráyańa defeated King Balii not by physical strength but by the strength of intellect. The word ba that we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal means that intellectual strength is the greatest strength, and it refers to Viśńu. ( 2 )

The word ba does not only mean one who is physically strong; it is equally applicable to one who is mentally or spiritually strong. That is why the word ba, which is used to mean the application of physical force, is also used to mean the application of mental or spiritual force. So, one of the meanings of ba, which we get by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bal is to create pressure, to create circumstantial pressure or to proceed according to a plan in order to attain some particular goal. Some people think that the word ba means to vilify someone. This is partly true. One can use the word ba when someone is vilified in order to pressurise that person into doing something. So the verbal root ba + d́a = ba means “to pressurise in order to attain a particular goal”.

t: The idea of pressurising reminds me of an anecdote. Have you heard of Palta, a well-known place? There lived a very simple, intelligent man. His name was probably Pat́olprasanna ( 1 ) Pal.
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna was a simple man who minded his own business, but his pious wife Smt. Begunbálá – well, who could withstand her speech! The torrential flow of words from her mouth was stronger than that of a western gale. Every day, she would religiously quarrel with Pat́olprasanna every fifteen minutes by the clock. She said that in this world, a man should work and one who did not work was sure to be ruined. The best kind of work was quarrelling. The kind of majesty that a serious quarrel invoked has hardly any comparison in the cosmos. When the quarrel reached its climax, Begunbálá would bring out her jewellery box, remove the ornaments from her body and put them in the box. Then she would put a lock on the box and check at least thrice to see that the box had been properly locked. After that, she would tie the key into a knot at the end of her saree and tuck it in her vest. Finally, she would hold the box in her hand and say, “Well, Mister, I am going now. I have decided to drown myself. Let me see which female ghost serves you food!”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna could only cast a dazed and vacant look at her. He could not utter a single word (rá-t́i káŕtaná ( 2 )) in his tension and anxiety.
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: With great zeal, Begunbálá would keep on quarrelling in a dance rhythm, sometimes moving five steps forward and sometimes retracing another four steps. During this time, who could stand up to that Amazonian figure of hers? Just by the side of the main entrance of the house was a huge pond. It was very deep. Begunbálá with her jewellery box would not go to that pond to drown herself. She would go through the back door to another pond, which was generally used for cleaning kitchen utensils. Even its deepest part was so shallow that a small pot could not sink in it. Begunbálá would move one step forward and say, “Mister, I am dying … Mister, I am sinking!” After that, she would stand still in a pose and warn her husband again, “Let me see who serves you food!” Then she would move another step further. Sometimes, Pat́olprasanna would ask in trepidation, “If you are going to die, what is the use of that jewellery box?”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Begunbala would reply, “I shall bury this jewellery box in the pond and then I shall turn into a Yaksha woman. I will see how strong you are. If you come down to this pond, I will catch hold of your big toe and drag you to hell. I will make you realise that Begunbálá is not an ordinary woman.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: At that moment, their only daughter, Jhiuṋgeráńii, would catch hold of Pat́olprasannaʼs hand and tell him, “Father, please drag my mother back. Canʼt you see that my mother is going to drown? O Father! What are you looking at? Just go and drag my mother back.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna would then say to Begunbálá, “That you are not an ordinary woman is known to the whole world, and as for me, I know it in my bones. You are a living goddess dropped from heaven. If you are not here, who is going to serve me food? For Godʼs sake, Oh mother of Jhiuṋge, donʼt make any more fuss, please come back! All the villagers have gathered on the banks of the pond. You may be shameless, but I do have some feelings of shame left in me still.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Begunbálá would then victoriously and majestically walk back home through the back door. After that, she would eat sumptuously delicious dishes like birir d́ál [a kind of pulse], baŕi-posta [a curry with opium seed], d́imer dálná [egg curry] and kuler ambal [sour broth of Indian plum] and, before going to bed, leave the leftovers for Pat́olprasanna. Pat́olprasanna was quite happy with that. The days when the quarrel reached a climax, Jhiuṋgeráńii would unequivocally support her mother.
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: According to psychology, whenever there is a quarrel between the father and the mother, a daughter generally supports the father. But this case was an exception because Jhiuṋgeráńii obtained her training in the art of quarrelling directly from her mother. Therefore, the mother had a stronger influence on her. Whenever the quarrel became serious, Jhiuṋgeráńii would say, “Má, you saw my father standing on the bank of the pond that day. He admitted that you were a goddess dropped from heaven. You must have seen that all the gods and goddesses have weapons in their hands. One who has two hands has weapons in both hands. One who has four hands has weapons in all four hands. One who has ten hands has weapons in all ten hands. So why should you fight empty-handed? Take either a belun [a roller for rolling chapattis] or a cyálákát́h [piece of wood] in one hand and an áṋshbaṋt́i or muŕojhyánt́á [a big knife to cut fish and a stubbed broom] in the other. Only then will this religious war be exciting; only then will this fighting be totally convincing.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Jhiuṋgeráńii would supply weapons to her mother. In that situation, Pat́olprasanna would recoil in fear. He would tie a handkerchief round his neck lest his throat was cut by the áṋshbaṋt́i. He would tie a napkin around it as well if it were readily available. In winter, he would put on a monkey cap to protect himself from the broom. But their son, Shreemán Dhyáṋŕash Kumar, was of a different temperament.

t: Well, let me tell you at this point that the actual name of Dhyáṋŕash Kumar was Dhyáṋŕash Ranjan. He had gone to Mumbai previously to join the film industry. When he was in Mumbai, he noticed that all the actors had the appellation “Kumar” to their names. So, in keeping with their style, he also changed his name to Dhyáṋŕash Kumar ( 3 ). Anyway, Dhyáṋŕash Kumar did not like these quarrels and clashes. When he found the situation unbearable, he would say, in a mix of Bengali and Hindi, “I canʼt stand all this! If you quarrel too much, I will run away from home and fling myself under a running train, or I will go to Mumbai again and join the film industry!”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: It is said that he had passed a few examinations in Hindi with credit. Fearing that the son might leave home, Begunbálá would on some occasions stop quarrelling, or at other times she would continue completely undeterred, accompanied by the oriental dance that she performed with the áṋshbaṋt́i and belun. This dance is certainly worth preserving in a colourful choreography.

t: Finally, the day came when Pat́olprasanna, unable to bear this kind of torture any longer, went to his Guru for help. The Guru whispered some secret solution into his ears. As he was about to leave, the Guru asked him several times, “Will you be able to do it? Are you sure you can do it?”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna replied, “Yes, sir, I will be able to. It is a question of life and death. How can I not do it?”

t: A few days later a quarrel began again – the same old, one-act play. Begunbálá took out the jewellery box from the iron chest, removed the ornaments from her body and put them in the box. After locking the box carefully, she pulled the small lock thrice to see whether it was properly secured. After that, she tied the key at the end of her saree and, instead of putting the end of the saree over her shoulder, she wrapped it round her waist and tucked the knot in it. It was safer to tie the saree up at the waist; otherwise, during the quarrel it might come off again and again. Then she started her dance to the rhythm of her quarrel.

t: Begunbálá threatened, “Today I must die! Must! It is not within your power to drag me back home. If you think that I shall commit suicide and go to hell while you go to heaven and relish sweet dishes and sleep snoringly, please remember – I wonʼt allow that. Whenever you take sweets and sleep on the cot in heaven, I will raise my hand and thrash you with the broom. I will completely spoil your joy of eating málpo [sweet pie] and sleeping. Look, has anybody met such a person in the world! The last time that I said to you during pújá, 'Printed sarees from Mushidabad are now available at the market. How glossy they are! How shimmering! Itʼs a joy to look at themʼ – shamelessly, I told him, ‘Please get me one.’ Look! This was his reply, 'Last year, I sustained a great loss in the production of potato crops. Donʼt be angry. Next year I will buy you one Murshidabad saree.ʼ The cheek of it! He has bought me only one cotton saree! And the saree was of such a poor quality that even the maidservant who works on the d́heṋki [the husking pedal] for the paddy turned her face away in disgust. He fulfilled my request with a cheap thing. The disease is not in the potatoes but in the head of this worthless man – minse ( 4 ); otherwise why should he give trouble to such a chaste and pious wife like me! I have been asking him for a long time to bring me a special water pot, khuro deoyá Khágŕái ghaṋt́i [a small pitcher with small stands, made in Khagra in Bengal]. But look! He keeps postponing it and now three months have passed. The manʼs brain is rotten. I canʼt tolerate it anymore. Oh, Náráyańa, please do something! Please send this man to the house of Yama on a chariot. I will arrange for abundant distribution of sweets, harir lut́, [scattering sweets in honour of Hari for the congregation of devotees to pick up] in your honour through the snub-nosed Banerjee (Boṋcá Báṋŕujje) of Baichee ( 5 ).”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna asked timidly, “Does anyone go to the house of Yama in a chariot? I heard that one is dragged with oneʼs legs tied up to the house of Yama, while one goes to heaven in a chariot.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Begunbálá rejoined acrimoniously, “Well, let me admit that you will go to heaven, but I have already told you that I wonʼt allow you to live in peace even in heaven.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: As usual, Begunbala started walking towards the backyard pond with the jewellery box in hand. Pat́olprasanna followed her along with his jewel of a daughter. Begunbálá moved two steps, stopped, and said, “Well, Mister, I am dying and drowning. Let me see who serves you food.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna looked on silently. In this way, Begunbálá reached the centre of the pond. She delivered her coup de grâce, “Mister, I am now dying and after death I shall trouble you seven hundred times more than what I have troubled you when alive.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Jhiuṋgeráńii appealed, “Father, Má is about to drown, please drag her back.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Pat́olprasanna said, “Ah! Itʼs a long cherished desire of your mother to die by drowning. Let that desire be fulfilled at least once. Let her die by drowning today. If a similar incident recurs tomorrow, I shall then drag her back.”
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: For quite some time, Begunbálá kept standing in that ankle-deep water and Pat́olprasanna kept looking on. Dark clouds gathered in the mind of Begunbálá while there was barely a flicker on the face of Pat́olprasanna. He was thinking that he had followed the advice of the Guru and it was working.
chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

chapterTitle: The Idea of Pressurising Fully Blossomed!

t: Begunbálá returned home. Since that day, Begunbálá has never quarrelled nor did she go with the jewellery box to drown herself in the backyard pond. The ba of Begunbálá came to nothing, while the ba of Pat́olprasanna fully blossomed. The story of ba ends here ( 6 ).
