t: One of the meanings of the word bha that we obtain by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root bha is “shining opulence”. There may be opulence of prestige, honour, money, quality or wisdom, but when that opulence is associated with welfare, then the word bha is used to indicate this. Please remember that opulence alone cannot elevate opulence to the category of bha. This means that the financial opulence of a rich man does not automatically come under the category of bha. Someoneʼs wealth may be bha while someone elseʼs may not be.
chapterTitle: Even a Hookah Can Be Useful for Charity

t: During my childhood, I heard that Manindra Chandra Nandi, the great, bountiful king of Kashim Bazar [Murshidabad District], never disappointed anyone. He thought that God had given him wealth to spend for public welfare. A time came when his estate sustained a huge loss on account of his charitable disposition, and the government acquired it under “Court of Words” [a legal term to acquire zaminderʼs property in British period]. In other words, his estate was run by government officers, and the king was given a limited monthly pension to meet the expenses of his family. As a result, the charity of the king was about to end and the poor people felt miserable. They prayed, “Let the wealth of the king grow more and more.” Since the king had spent his wealth on public welfare, this kind of wealth may be considered as bha.
chapterTitle: Even a Hookah Can Be Useful for Charity

t: One day during that period, a poor man came to him with the hope of getting some money. The king was then virtually a pauper. At that moment, he was smoking his silver-plated hookah. On hearing the sad tale of the poor man, he felt pity for him and said, “Look, I donʼt have any money on me. You had better take this silver-plated hookah. Please sell it and make use of the money you get from it.”
chapterTitle: Even a Hookah Can Be Useful for Charity

t: There are many people in this world who possess huge wealth, but who neither feed themselves nor feed others. Their wealth does not come under the category of bha.

I knew a big merchant, Sethjii ( 1 ), who sat on a hill of money. He always kept a vigilant watch to see that his money was not drained away by any means. He always bought secondhand garments from the market for his children. He would present the shop-soiled and torn sarees that were rejected by the shopkeepers and sold very cheap to his wife, Papaŕkumárii Devii (pápaŕ means “a round, thin snack made from pulse” – parpat́ii > pappad́i > pappaŕ >pápaŕ), and would advise her, “If anybody asks, say that the saree got torn accidentally by pricking the cooking spud while cooking pilau (poláo).”

For breakfast, Sethjii ate parched maize (jandá ká lábá) but would tell people that unless there were specially prepared sweet dishes like kalakand ( 2 ) and ghior [a sweet dish rich in clarified butter], a breakfast would not be delicious.

After so many years, I canʼt recollect the exact name of Sethjii. It was probably Seth Jhabarmal Jhunjhunwala. He hailed from Jhalawar [Rajasthan]. Sethjii was the richest man in town. Nobody dared to mention his name early in the morning because they feared that they would have nothing but parched maize to eat for the whole day if they did. Sethjiiʼs son was a schoolmate of my brother. His name was Natthumal Jhunjhunwala. Natthumal was very good in his studies. All the townsfolk felt very happy when he was promoted to class VIII, scoring the highest marks in all subjects. When awarding first prize to him, the Headmaster expressed his joy in glowing language. He said, “I hope that one day, this boy will bring name not only to my school but also to the whole country.” But “Oh, brother! What a strange thing, I have never seen such a thing in my life!”.
Strangely enough, Natthumal felt sad and a greater darkness clouded the countenance of Jhabarmal. I asked Jhabarmal, “Why are you so visibly worried on such a day of joy?”

He said, “Look here, Mr. Sarkar, if after completing his education my son becomes a university professor or a government officer, who will look after my business? It would have been much better if he had failed several examinations, because then I could have discontinued his studies on those grounds. Moreover, do you know, Mr. Sarkar, I have a genuine apprehension that he will form a movement with my factory workers to seek higher salaries. He will set them against me; he will form a workersʼ union with them. So I am thinking what to do. I have discussed the matter with my wife. She said, 'When the boy is so good, so bright, let him continue to study. If you are reluctant to spend money on him, I can send him to my paternal house. My brothers will bring him up.”

That day, Sethjii had serious altercations with his wife. The wife of Sethjii did not eat anything on that day on account of her anger, sadness and disappointment. That of course made Sethjii rather happy because it saved him the cost of one dayʼs meal for one person.
One day, I eventually ran into Natthumal at the market. He came to me weeping and said, “Sarkar Saheb, I shall die by flinging myself under a running train.”
I asked, “Why so! You are such a small boy, how did such an evil thought occur to you?”

He replied, “My father says that he cannot afford my educational expenses anymore. The business is not running well. He has sustained a loss of Rs.1 lakh [one hundred thousand rupees] in the corn business.”
I asked him, “Is it a fact?”
He said, “No, Sarkar Saheb, it is not at all true. Actually he has made a profit of two and half lakhs. But in the fake account, he has shown a loss of one lakh to evade income and sales taxes.”
I asked, “Tell me what can be done then.”
Natthumal said, “Sarkar Saheb, please put in a word to my father.”
I said, “But your mother told me that she wanted to send you to your maternal uncle for further studies. Does your father have any objection to it?”
He replied, “Father said, 'If he becomes educated, he will become a clerk (bábu) instead of a Seth and my business will go to seed.ʼ”

Looking at Natthumalʼs face, I felt a heaviness in my heart, but nothing could be done because in those days there was no “free students home” for meritorious students. So I could not do anything for him.

Finally, with great reluctance, Natthumal started to work in his fatherʼs office. His job was to write something in the fat, red ledger books. Whenever he saw me walking in the street, he would lower his face in shame. Such a situation was unbearable to me. Since then, he has never come within my sight. Jhabarmal had aborted a fine talent.

One day, Jhabarmalʼs father-in-law (samadhii or beyái ( 3 )) [the father-in-law or uncle-in-law of a son or daughter] came from a faraway land to visit him. Jhabarmal was completely perplexed. Who knows how long his beyái will stay? One cannot treat the beyái with simple chapatti made of Bulrush millet and chilli pickle. He arrived at around 10.30 in the morning. Jhabarmal stretched out both hands to welcome his beyái and said, “Welcome! Most welcome! How gracious you are to have set foot in the house of a poor man like me. Although my business is passing through a dull stage at the moment, on seeing you, I forget my sorrow. You are the right person to understand my sorrow. I cannot perhaps give you the kind of welcome that I could have, had my business been roaring. Even then, I shall try to do my best.”
The beyái said, “How does that matter, how does that matter, really? Please donʼt worry about it Sethjii.”

Jhabarmal said, “Look here, my honourable beyái. In our house, the cooking is done by 10 AM. But since you have come, the stove must be ignited again to cook for you. You are my esteemed beyái and some delicate dishes must be prepared for you, whatever may be my present financial condition. It will take at least two hours to do the cooking. But I canʼt keep you starving for such a long time. In fact, the water of my courtyard well is very good. For the time being, at least take a glass of water and cool yourself down. After that, come along with me. There is an excellent restaurant, the best restaurant of this place, the umda ( 4 ) restaurant, nearby. Its name is 'Absolutely Pure Parot́á [A thin bread fried in oil or clarified butter] Shopʼ. They serve pure vegetarian meals cooked in pure ghee [clarified butter].”

In spite of his fatigue from the journey, the beyái started for 'the very pure parot́á shopʼ with his son-in-law. Jhabarmal told the restaurant manager, “This is my honourable beyái. He is a very wealthy man. He never eats anything on someone elseʼs account. I am such a close relative of his, but he wonʼt even eat on my account. So serve him all the best items that you have on your menu – kacaurii, kaŕi baŕi, ratuyá, ghior, kalákanda, sábudána ká pápaŕ, rábŕi and málái [all are Indian food delicacies; kalákanda, rábŕi, malái are made from thickened milk]. Moreover, you should also serve him anything else he may ask for.
After seating him down for lunch, Jhabarmalji said, “My dear sir, I have some work left in the shop, so please allow me to leave.”

Before leaving, he told the manager of the hotel, “Although on principle he does not eat anything on someone elseʼs account, even then he is my near relative and so I canʼt let him do that. Let him make the payment now. But I shall later reimburse him by forcing the money into his pocket. Since he is my guest, he must eat on my account.”

Then he told his beyái, “Dear sir, please eat to your heartʼs content and please donʼt fill your stomach by drinking water. Water you will take in my house. Nowhere on earth will you find such digestive water.”
After that, Jhabarmal returned home and told his wife, “Come, let us all take our lunch very quickly. We must finish our meal before beyái returns.”
This kind of man, Jhabarmal – it is immaterial to others whether he has property or not. So his wealth does not come under the category of bha.

Money does not necessarily bring charisma to a person, and possession of money cannot necessarily be considered as wealth. Most of you know about Mr Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje [literally, the begging and licking Chatterjee] of our Cuṋcuŕo-Carakdángá [Chinsurah-Charakdanga]. Nobody knows how much money he has. It is said that once Kuber [the God of wealth], while counting his money, fell senseless on account of excessive strain. Now, can we call the wealth of this Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje lustrous? Does it come under the category of bha? No, it does not. Let me tell you an anecdote.

Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje had sixty-four houses in Cuṋcuŕá [Chinsurah] and Cannagar [Chandannagar and Catra] and he was very cautious in his speech. He tried to suppress the hollowness of his mind by talking in a heavy voice. He had to speak in a heavy voice because –
Yár áche báŕii tár kathá bhárii bhárii,
Yár áche dhán tár kathá t́án t́án,
Yar áche t́áká tár kathá báṋká báṋká.
[One who has a house speaks in a heavy voice,
One who has paddy speaks in a drawling voice,
One who has money speaks in a devious manner.]
The village people own paddy and they speak in a drawling tone. A moneyed person never speaks straight; he or she always speaks in a devious manner.

Whatever the case may be, our Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje kept on buying houses one after another. But he had no heir who could enjoy his property after his demise. In his family line, he was the only member (baḿshadhar). He always carried his bamboo stick (baḿsha) because in both senses – common parlance and etymology – he was the carrier of his line [baḿsha means both a line and a bamboo stick]. It is not that anyone who has money will buy a house. In fact, different communities have different preferences. About who does what on acquiring substantial money, it is said:
Bauṋgáliir báŕii, sáheber gáŕii,
Miiṋásáheber háṋŕi, meyemánuśer sháŕii.
[A Bengali buys a house, an Englishman buys a car,
A Muslim buys a cooking pot, a woman buys a saree.]

On acquiring a good amount of money, a Bengali buys a house. An Englishman, once he has enough money, will buy at least a secondhand car, if not the latest model. When luck favours a Muslim, he begins to eat delicious dishes and spends his money on food. In other words, he spends his money on cooking pots. And, well, it is not desirable to talk much about a womanʼs fondness for sarees because it is risky to do so; it may disturb domestic peace.

Anyway, money was the be-all and end-all of our Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje. He would say, “Where is the time to think about anything else? All my time is spent checking the amount of interest accrued on my money.”

One fine morning, Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje was struck by a feeling of renunciation. He thought, “What is all this money for? Let me at least eat some good dishes today. Let me eat enough for a lifetime.” He then called Bhola, who worked for him as a general assistant.

Cáoyá-Cát́á ate puiṋsháker ( 1 ) caccaŕi and rice. Why should he buy puiṋshák from the market? He made Bhola cultivate it in the courtyard of the house. Bhola cleaned the utensils, did the cooking, cleaned the house, went to the market to shop and to sell puiṋshák because the quantity of puiṋshák that grew in Cáoyá-Cát́áʼs courtyard was a little more than the needs of one person. In order to induce Bhola to sell puiṋshák at a high price, he told him, “I will pay your salary from the proceeds of the sale of puiṋshák.”
Anyway, on the day of that feeling of renunciation, he called Bhola and said, “Look here Bhola, today I feel like eating some delicacies. So you bring one seer of chánár poláo.”
Bhola, beside himself with joy, said, “I shall bring it in a jiffy, I shall bring it right now! I shall return as soon as I go. Please give me the money.”

After a brief pause, Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “Well, why chánár poláo [salted delicacy made of fresh cheese]? Let me take chánár páyes [sweet made of fresh cheese] today. Is it available here or do you have to go to Chandannagar?”
Bhola replied, “Yes, sir, we can get it here. There is a particular shop in Kharobajar where it is available.”
Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “Kharobajar is quite far from here. You had better do one thing. Today, you bring one seer of kśiirer málpo [another sweet made of condensed milk].”
Bhola said, “I will bring it – right now. Please give me the money. I will run all the way and get it for you.”

Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “Now that all is said and done, I remember having seen an advertisement in the newspaper the other day about a new kind of sweet called rasamádhurii. But can we find it in our Chuchura market?”
Bhola said, “I will enquire about it. Even if it is not available in Chuchura, it will certainly be available in Chandannagar.”

Cáoyá-Cát́á put his hand on his right cheek and pondered a while. Then he put his hand on the left cheek and pondered a while. Then he said, “Look, let us not do that today. Today, you bring pyáṋj-phuluri [onion chop]. I hope you understand the difference between peṋyájii and pyáṋj-phuluri?”
Bhola answered, “No, sir.”

Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “If there is more besan [gram flour] than onion, then it is called pyáṋj-phuluri. It is fried in a lot of oil with a honeycombed iron ladle. But in peṋyájii, only a minimal amount of besan is used and it is fried in a flat pan with very little oil sprinkled on it. Sometimes, the vendors selling fried stuff pass off the peṋyájii as pyáṋj-phuluri to make more profit. So make sure that what you bring is actually pyáṋj-phuluri.”
Bhola said, “Sir, rest assured, I will check thoroughly before I buy.”
Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “Yes, be very careful. One piece
of pyáṋj-phuluri will be enough for my breakfast for two days.”
Bhola said, “So I am off. Please give me the money.”

Cáoyá-Cát́á said, “Money? Anybody can bring it with money! Canʼt you bring it without money even for a day? All the vendors know us. Canʼt you bring one piece of pyáṋj-phuluri just by nagging them?”
After some time, Bhola reappeared before Cáoyá-Cát́á with an empty sal leaf. Cáoyá-Cát́á asked, “Whatʼs the matter? What have you brought? Peṋyájii as pyáṋj-phuluri?”
Bhola said, “The shopkeeper told me that everybody takes peṋyájii on a sal leaf; you can give this sal leaf without the peṋyájii on it to your master.”

Yes, we were talking about the notorious Cáoyá-Cát́á [the amusing name means “always asking for”] Cát́ujje. He was an eminent person in Chinsura-Carakdaunga. I hope some of you know my acquaintance, Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal Hotá. Some of you must know him. (A farmer by profession, he hailed from Halimpur, Hooghly District, Khatian [ledger] No. 3 Plot No. 300). Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal [Hyáḿlá means “greedy”] was not a bad boy, but he was particularly fond of attending feasts. Quite often, he used to wangle an invitation to a feast by asking for it. Sometimes, he would eat at a feast given on the occasions of various rituals, such as shráddha [obsequies] and paite [the ceremony of putting on the holy thread sacramentally for the first time] without an invitation. He had long hair. While eating, he would bend his head in such a way that his face was screened by his hair. The host, when checking the guests to see who were invited and who were not, could not confirm whether he had actually been invited because his face could not be seen. His younger brother, Barśá Bádal, was not so resourceful. As a result, he was not lucky enough to get invitations to feasts.
One day, while I was brushing my teeth with a margosa brush [twig] wearing only a lungi [long loincloth worn by men], I saw Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal walking on the street. He looked visibly happy.
I asked “Hello, Hyáḿlá whatʼs the matter? You are looking so happy today!”
With a still happier face he said, “Today, early in the morning, I managed to get an invitation to a feast.”
I said, “So this morning you had a very good beginning.”
He said, “Yes, sir.”
I asked, “Where? To whose house are you invited?”
He said, “To the house of Cáoyá-Cát́á Cát́ujje.”
I said, “How strange! He never spends any money on anyone; he only asks for it. How come he has invited you all of a sudden today?”
Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal looked worried.
I said, “Come what may, you ask your mother to prepare at least some rice and broth for you for the night.”
Hyaḿlá gave a vacant look.
I said, “At the same time, you do one more thing. You talk to Cáoyá-Cát́á and ascertain whether he has really invited you.”
After some time, I saw Hyaḿlá coming to me again. His face was as dark as a moonless night.
I asked him, “Whatʼs the matter? Why is your face so clouded?”

He said, “I asked Cáoyá-Cát́á, 'Am I really invited today?ʼ Cáoyá-Cát́á at once replied, 'Certainly, of course. Not once, but hundred times, yes.ʼ After a brief pause, Cáoyá-Cát́á told me, 'Man has progressed a lot in observing formalities. Whatever it is, whether one sincerely likes formality or not, it is written on the wedding invitation card, ‘Blessing in place of formality is desirable’. But actually, everybody wants formality instead of blessing. You will notice that there is a practice of keeping a written record of who has presented what to the bride and the bridegroom in wedding homes. Obviously, such an account is maintained because there is a hankering, in the deepest recesses of the mind for these presents. Not only that, you will see that if somebodyʼs marriage takes place towards the end of the month, the ceremony of bau-bhát [the ceremony of a bride serving food for the first time to her husbandʼs kinsfolk] is not held then because by the end of the month, everybodyʼs pocket is empty. The guests may not come at all because they are unable to give presents. And those who do come would not be able to give costly presents. Keeping this in view, bau-bhát is arranged at the beginning of the next month a few days after the marriage. At that time, the guests are quite solvent. Moreover, not much money is spent on feeding because it is written on the invitation card that the entertainment of the guests will be in keeping with the rules of ‘guest control’. It means that just by giving a light refreshment, it is possible to squeeze an expensive gift.

'Come what may – do you understand Hyáḿlá – I donʼt like those formalities and I think you also donʼt like them. But you are an intelligent, educated boy; you canʼt go to the invitation empty-handed. You must bring a few packets of canácur and d́álmut́ [snacks] in your pocket. In my house, there are good stainless steel plates and tumblers. I would naturally expect that you will put the canácur on the plate and eat it with satisfaction. In case there is load shedding [power cut] at that time, I shall entertain you, my guest, by fanning you with a hand fan. The well in my courtyard has the best water in Chinsura. It is not salty like the water of the Ganges. Whatever you eat will be immediately digested. Even if you bring four or five packets, you will see that by the time you reach home, they will all be digested.ʼ”
Hyáḿlá Hoṋdal told me, “After listening to Cáoyá-Cát́á, I felt simply dazed and stupefied. Even in this hot summer, I am shivering with cold.”
The story of Cáoyá-Cát́á ends here.

In the consonantal scheme of alphabets, the first letter in the ka group is ka and the last letter in the pa group is ma. Now the question is: why does ka come first and ma last? This world revolves around the process of creation, preservation and destruction. The seed of creation is a; that is why a comes first in the vowels. First creation, and only then do the rest follow. After that is u, the seed of preservation. So creation is spread over these three sounds. The combination of these three sounds is called ońḿ (a + u + m = ońḿ).
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Ka is the seed of action of Brahma. In other words, one part of the Supreme Brahma continues to exist as the cause while the other part is manifested in action. One part is the cause and the other part is the effect or objectivated cause. That is why this ka is called saḿvrttibodhicitta in Buddhist philosophy. Since ka is the seed of action, ka is therefore the first consonant; and since ma is the seed of destruction, ma is the last consonant.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: I was talking about ouṋḿkára – a + u + m = ońḿ. But this om is meant for the manifested world. If one wants to use the seed of some positive sound for both the manifested and the unmanifested, then om will not do; one has to write oṋḿ [like Bengali symbol]. In this case, the candrabindu [the diacritical mark of a point in the crescent moon indicating a nasalised sound] connotes Nirguńa Brahma [Brahma without attributes]. This Brahma without attributes cannot be verbalised in utterance. So, in orthography, one first uses a point (a point has a position but no magnitude) and the longish sign that looks like a crescent moon under the point indicates the transformation from the negative to the positive aspect of attributes. In Sanskrit, it is called náda, that is, nirguńa saḿsthiti [the state of non-attributes] is transformed into Saguńa Brahma [the state of attributes] with the help of náda or sound. Please remember that it is not exactly a candrabindu [a point with a curve suggestive of the crescent moon]. It is something like the Bengali iishvara sign (a symbol put before the name of a deceased person). According to old custom, this nádabinducihna is used before the name of a dead person. When reading this nádabindu, we read it as iishvara. When a man is alive, the word shrii is used before his name; for example, Shrii Kumud Chandra Maiti. But the prefix Shrii cannot be used before his name after his death. The name Kumud Chandra Maiti will be written just after nadabindu and the name will be read as iishvara Kumud Chandra Maiti.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Another name of oṋḿkára is prańava, the etymological meaning of which is “that which propels towards the destination.” You are probably aware of the fact that in ancient times, in that age of superstition, not everyone had the right to articulate the word oṋḿkára. The outcastes and women were not only disallowed from uttering the word oṋḿ, even their right to hear the word was constrained. Hearsay has it that if any of them heard the oṋḿkára sound, molten lead would be poured into their ears to make them completely deaf. Verily, what an age of superstition it was! Such superstitions pervaded all walks of life. It was not only women who were tortured on account of this; men suffered no less. A story of social superstition comes to mind. The story is about one Subuddhi Roy of the Pathan dynasty.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Subuddhi Roy was the Prime Minister of Bengal during the reign of the Pathans. In addition to his political stature, he enjoyed great social prestige as well. On one particular occasion, some water from a Muslimʼs badná [a small pitcher with a slender spout] accidentally touched his face. The Brahman pundits convened a meeting. They unanimously resolved that it was a serious sin, a serious crime. Subuddhi Roy would have to perform a ceremonial expiation. Oh, I forgot to tell you that Subuddhi Roy at that time was the head of the Brahman community, a representative of the Brahmans.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: As the Brahman community rose in arms against Subuddhi Roy, he became frightened to the extreme. He was made to seek the counsel of the pundits of Nabadwip [Navadviip] for the necessary mode of expiation. The pundits of Nabadwip gave the verdict that he had to perform tuśáńal práyashcitta [expiation with fire made from husks or chaff]. In tuśáńal práyashcitta, the guilty person had to stand before the fire when it was fully ablaze. The husks would be spread over an area covering sixty-four times the height of the person. The sinner or guilty person had to walk barefoot on it. If the sinner survived the ordeal, the expiation would be accomplished. And if the sinner died, the matter ended there.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Terrified of this tuśáńal práyashcitta, Subuddhi Roy went to Kashi [Benares] to seek counsel from the pundits there. Subuddhi Roy, the Prime Minister, thought that since the pundits of Kashi were great scholars, they might recommend some other form of expiation. When he reached Kashi, he explained everything to these scholars.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Práyascitta puchilá teṋ pańd́iter stháne,
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Tárá kay tapta ghrta kháiyá cháŕa práńe.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: [He asked the pundits about the mode of expiation,
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: They said, “You should die by gulping down hot ghee.”]
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: The pundits of Kashi remarked that the scholars of Nabadwip knew nothing. The scriptural prescription was hot ghee. One had to drink ghee after making it very hot. And one had to continue drinking it till death. This was known as “taptaghrta prayashcitta” [expiation with hot ghee]. Subuddhi Roy saw that in either case, whether you were killed by Rama or by Ravana, it would be a premature death. Rather, it was better to die by drowning in the Ganges.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Prime Minister Subuddhi Roy proceeded towards the Ganges. At that time, Mahaprabhu Chaitanya Dev [Caetanyadeva] was on his way from Nabadwip to Brindavana after a brief soujourn in Kashi. When he saw Subuddhi Roy in that condition, he thought, “The man is apparently educated and honourable, yet darkness clouds his countenance and worry is writ large on his forehead. He is going towards the Ganges at this unusual time – the matter is suspicious. It appears from his face that he is a man from Bengal.” He asked him, “Whatʼs the matter? Who are you? Where are you going?”
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Subuddhi Roy broke down in tears and told him the whole story. Mahaprabhu Chaitanya Dev was stunned to hear about the inhuman behaviour of the pundits. He condemned them in very sharp language, and then said:
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Prabhu kay ihá haite yáo brndavana,
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Nirantar krśńanáma kara saḿkiirtan.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Ek námáveshe tomár páp dhuye yábe,
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Ár nám laite krśńa sharań páibe.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: [From here you go to Brindavana and continuously count the beads in the name of Krśńa. With the first utterance of the name of Krśńa, your sin will be washed away, and with the second utterance you will be taken into the fold of Krśńa.]
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: Mahaprabhu said, “Donʼt fall into the clutches of those impostors. Go to Brindavana. Always remember Krśńa. The [supposed] stain of that water from the Muslim badná will vanish as soon as you utter the word ‘Krśńa’ once. When you utter the name for the second time, you will realise that you are in the fold of Krśńa.”
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: The life of Subuddhi ( 1 ) Roy was saved. Mahaprabhu Chaitanya Dev saved his life from being sacrificed at the altar of social tortures.
chapterTitle: Subuddhi Roy in the Clutches of Kubuddhi Roy

t: One meaning of the Sanskrit verbal root mada is “what gives pleasure in sucking”. Etymologically, it means water, cordial, sharbat [sweet drink], hyacinth, fruit juice and any kind of fluid which comes under the category of drinks. The kind of thirst that one feels after consuming the items mentioned above is called mada + d́a = ma. For example, one feels thirsty when one takes chátu [flour made of barley, pigeon-pea, maize, etc.] in a small quantity of water. Again, one feels thirsty when taking poláo [a highly spiced dish of rice and meat boiled in clarified butter]. This kind of thirst for water is called jaltán.
Have you heard the story of the acute thirst of Brajaballabh Basak of Balagarh? In case you have not heard it, let me repeat the story.

Brajaballah Basak lived in Balagarh, his ancestral home (bhadrásan). ( 1 ) However, the close friends of Brajaballabh Basak lived some distance away. Bijit Báṋŕujje, a very intimate friend of his, lived in Bana Hooghly and Bijit Basu, another intimate friend, lived in Bajeshibpur. It was a time when the son of Bijit Báṋŕujje, who had just completed his education, joined the government department where food grains were collected and stored after purchasing them according to their weight. The son of Bijit Basu, who had just passed the M.A. examination, was about to join the post of a professor in a college in Hooghly.

One day, after Brajaballabh Basak returned from his morning walk, his wife Seyánásundarii said, “Please listen, my dear. Your friend Bijitbabu has just sent a message that the bau-bhát [the ceremony of a bride serving food for the first time to her husbandʼs kinsfolk] of his son will be held tonight and you must attend the ceremony; he will feel very sad if you donʼt. He could not come to invite you personally because of his very busy schedule. Otherwise, he would have come to fetch you.”
Brajaballab Basak asked Seyánásundari, “Do you remember the place he mentioned – Bana Hooghly or Bájeshibpur?”
Seyánásundari replied, “I didnʼt ask so much because the man who came said, 'Bijitbabu is very close to Brajababu. If you just mention his name, he will understand immediatelyʼ.”
Brajaballabh said, “Well, thatʼs right, but did he say Bijit Basu or Bijit Báṋrujje?”
Seyánásundari answered, “That too I did not ask because the manager said 'Braijababu will understand as soon as he hears the name of the host, you donʼt have to say anything moreʼ.”

Brajaballabh was in a quandary. He now applied his common sense. The son of Bijit Báṋŕujje was in government service. Efforts must have been made to marry him after he had obtained the job. So it was more likely that it was his marriage. Bijit Basuʼs son had yet to commence his job as a professor. A search will be made for a good bride after he joins the post. Then there will be the dowry discussion. Then the horoscopes will be studied and compared to see the compatibility of the match and only then can the marriage be held. So it was a 99.9% probability that it was the marriage of the son of Bijit Báṋŕujje to which he had been invited.

To go to Bajeshibpur, one had to cross the Ganges because there was no direct train from Balagarh to Bajeshibpur, but one did not need to cross the Ganges in order to go to Bana Hooghly. But what could Brajaballabh Basak do? After all, he was a close friend, and a friend is dearer than a relative. So, somehow, he reached Bana Hooghly a little before sunset. Since it was the marriage of a friendʼs son, he could not just go and sit at the dinner table like an outsider. If necessary, he would have to help to knead the dough, make the luci and he might even have to fry it, with a towel wrapped round his waist. Or he may have to serve the food with a bucket of dál [pulse] in the left hand and a ladle in the right. He would also have to carry a gámchá [country towel] on one shoulder to mop up the sweat from time to time. So it was very necessary to arrive a little early.

Brajaballab Basak arrived at Bana Hooghly. What was this! The house of Bijit Báṋrujje did not look at all like a wedding house. There was no light outside. A low-power bulb was dimly lit in the drawing room at the front. He had to knock on the door as it was not open.
Bijit Báṋŕujje said, “Welcome! Welcome Braja! Your company is so scarce these days!”

What Brajaballabh saw on entering the room only deepened his doubts. This house was certainly not a wedding house. He quickly hid his misgivings and exchanged a few formalities with Bijit Báṋŕujje. Bijit Báṋŕujje looked visibly drowsy. It was about a quarter to nine at night.

Bijit Báṋŕujje apologised while yawning, “These days, I generally have an early supper and, you understand, now that I am old, many things donʼt suit me. I retire at night just after taking a little khai [parched rice prepared by frying paddy] and milk. Thatʼs quite light you know.”
Brajaballabh Basak said, “Well, I have been trying to leave since a while. I cannot tell you how happy I am on seeing you after a long time. Well, I am off. By the way, what is your son doing now?”

Bijit Báṋrujje said, “My son is doing his service very sincerely and he has had a promotion as well. He could have got another promotion but that has been kept in abeyance because he could not pass the Hindi examination.”
Brajaballabh Basak asked, “What about the marriage of your son?”

Bijit Báṋŕujje said, “The search is on for a suitable bride but the problem is, when we like the bride we canʼt come to an agreement about ‘give and take’, and when we agree on the ‘give and take’, we do not like the prospective bride. But I hope we will be able to arrange the marriage by the next Mágh [the tenth month of the Bengali calendar, from the middle of January to the middle of February]. You are sure to get the news well in advance.”

Brajaballab Basak returned home. On hearing the knock at the door, Seyánásundari opened the door. Brajaballabh entered his home and looked at his wife with a touch of sadness on his face. Seyánásundari asked, “How was the feast? What did they prepare? Luci or poláo [poláo: rice and ghee rich preparation]?”

Brajaballabh said, “First, give me a glass of cold water, please.” Brajaballabh sank into the chair and placed his hand under his right cheek. He loudly heaved a deep sigh. He muttered to himself, “Both luci and polao.”
Seyánásundari returned with the glass of water and said to Brajaballabh Basak, “You donʼt have to tell me what they prepared, I understand.”
Brajaballabh said, “Tell me, what did they prepare?”
Seyánásundari said, “Of course poláo.”
Brajaballabh asked, “How did you know?”
Seyánásundari answered, “That much I know. I know, my dear, that eating poláo makes one feel parched.”

Food (in the sense of the verbal root ma) which does not cause any trouble upon its ingestion is called ma. This kind of food does not require much chewing and usually goes down the throat almost as soon as it has been put into the mouth; for example, birikaláyer dál [blackgram pulse], kuler ambal, pát́ or pát-shák [green leaves of jute plant] with a touch of salt and pepper and items prepared with basella are quite wholesome and can easily be eaten. That is why, by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root mada or by adding the suffix ka to the verbal root má, we get the word ma to mean this kind of food.

I trust you know the story. I mean, the story of the wife of a Brahman who was very fond of basella. You certainly know it but let me remind you of it once more. I remember the story of basella particularly when talking about ma.

There lived a Brahman and his wife. The Brahman was a very good man, as simple and ever cheerful as Lord Shiva. His wife was also a very good person, but she was rather fond of eating – in particular, the attraction of basella was irresistible to her. Ut́hone yedike cái keval puiṋ dekhite pái [in whichever direction of the courtyard I look, only basella comes to view]. The Brahman also ate basella but did not like it much. After eating some pántá bhát [stale rice] and hot beguni [a fried snack prepared by dipping slices of brinjal in a thin paste of pulse powder] with a sprinkle of salt and pepper, he would leave the house for various kinds of work. His wife took care of the household chores. After some time, it was noticed that the Brahman was getting more and more emaciated while his wife was getting heavier by the day. The people of the locality enquired, “Oh Brahman, what has happened to you? You are getting thinner and thinner and your wife is becoming heavier and heavier! What is the mystery? Certainly, after treating you with a pot of stale rice and packing you off, your wife must be preparing seven hundred kinds of delicious food and eating them with relish afterwards.”
The Brahman said, “Fie, Fie! Donʼt talk like that. When I hear such words, I feel like plugging my ears. My wife is the greatest woman in the world. She is not capable of doing things like that.”

But people continued to say the same thing again and again. One day, the Brahman thought, “Since these people are so insistent, let me verify it.” That day, the Brahman, after going out through the main door, stealthily re-entered the house through the back door, tiptoed into the kitchen and lay down in the attic. He could not breathe heavily lest his wife, on hearing the sound of breathing, suspected that there was someone else present in the room. Most of the time, the Brahman had to put a silencer on his mouth to suppress the sounds of sneezing and coughing.

The Brahman kept watching and watching and watching. His wife, meanwhile, collected a huge pile – about one maund [82 lbs] of basella, basella leaves and basella paste and prepared a dry dish of basella. She then poured a liberal quantity of oil and fried basella stems and the bones of bhet́kii fish [a large, flat fish found in rivers] into it, dipped some green basella leaves in the basella paste and fried them like phuluri, made a paste of raw poppy seeds with salt and pepper, mixed it with boiled basella and made basella posta [basella-poppy seed preparation]. After that, she prepared shukto [bitter broth], postor baŕá [fried poppy seeds], jhiuṋe posta, chánár dálná [fresh cheese curry], jhál, jhol, ghant́a, caccaŕi, chyáṋcŕá, diḿler chakká, kuler ambal, birirdál [different delicious preparations], different kinds of pies and, finally, ciṋŕer páyes [a sweet prepared with milk and beaten rice] with nalenguŕ [date palm raw sugar].

Well, that was only about the cooking or the first part of the ritual. After that, she entered the kitchen, arranged seven hundred pots and collected a huge quantity of rice piled so high that a cat would not be able to jump over it. Thus, she was engaged in completing the second part of the ritual. So many things! How can they be eaten with one hand! So the wife of the Brahman started using both hands.

It took quite a few hours before she finished her meal, leaving a huge pile of chewed-up food. The woman said to herself, “Truly, can this be called eating? Today, what I have put into my mouth is just chicken feed.” Then, a dark thought came to her mind. She thought, “I have taken so much pains to cook, more pains to eat and now, look, I should somehow make my way to the pond to quickly wash my mouth and then lie down to chew the betel leaves while someone else cleans the leftovers. But, alas, there is no one to help me!” The woman kept muttering to herself:
Sholak molak Báṋasher gajá,
Bhátt́i pele pet́t́i sojá,
Pánt́i pele áro majá,
Pet bale mágo,
Ámáy niye shogo.
[It has been rightly remarked that a betel leaf tastes better when the stomach is filled with cooked rice. The stomach then seems to ask the person to lie down and relax.]

But there was no second person in the house – neither a crow nor a cuckoo, neither a frog nor a lizard to pick up the utensils, clean them, sweep the room and mop up the stove. After eating so much food, did one really feel like performing these tasks? Twice, the woman tried to stand up with the support of her hands. But it was not so easy to get up. She weighed two maunds before eating, and after eating she had become four full maunds. The woman started humming a tune:
D́halá d́halá puiṋyer pátá maluk cáler bhát,
Kheye deye rainu base ke phyálábe pát!
[After I have eaten a bellyful of fine rice along with curry made of delicious basella leaves, I keep on sitting, waiting for somebody to clean up the place!]

Hiding in the attic, the Brahman somehow tolerated everything all this while. But when he heard his wife singing the rhyme, he could no longer control himself. His whole frame began to shake in anger, and even in that bitter cold he started sweating all over. He struck his stick on the attic floor and blurted out:
Mácay áche bámun t́hákur joŕ kariye hát,
Ot́ho ámár báper t́hákur hám phyálengá pát.
[The Brahman is waiting in the attic. I now request with folded hands, You, most revered paternal deity, please get up, I shall clean the place.]

While saying this, he jumped down and lightly beat his wife with his stick. The womanʼs stomach was already full. The pit́he páyes [the sweet dishes] were almost near her throat. So even though she was beaten lightly, her stomach burst open and out came all the tasty food – basella, pit́he, páyes, etc. How can one survive after the stomach bursts open?

The woman died. When he saw that his wife was dead, the Brahman started wailing. While crying loudly, he kept saying, “Please come here, whoever hears me, come and see at least once. Alas, what have I done! I did not want to kill my wife. I just wanted to frighten her, to discipline her. I never would have thought that she would die and cause me to be overwhelmed with sorrow. Please come, whoever hears me. Please come and see what has happened.”

Everybody loved the Brahman. They all rushed to the place. But nothing could be done now because the woman was absolutely dead. There was one old kaviráj [Ayurvedic doctor] in the crowd. When he heard the Brahmanʼs wails, he took pity on him. He said, “Well, let me see the patient. How long has the woman been dead?”
The Brahman sobbed, “It has been about an hour.”

The kaviráj said, “Please bring me a medical needle and some twine thread. Let me give a last try. Let me stitch up the stomach and see if the woman can be revived.” After saying this, the kaviráj put a thread in the needle and stitched up the stomach of the woman. After some time, the woman came back to life. After some more time, she opened her eyes. The joy of all around knew no bounds.

The Brahman wiped the tears from his eyes and said, “Oh, my dear wife, so you have come back! What a great occasion of rejoicing, what a great occasion of rejoicing indeed! Should you really leave us like that without giving any proper notice?”
Everybody was laughing. Everybody was happy. But the woman was shedding tears incessantly. The people asked, “What is this, oh lady, why are you weeping on such an occasion of joy?”
The woman replied, “Frankly speaking, I do not want to live like this! I donʼt like to live a life like this. Dying is better than living like this!”
Everyone asked, “Whatʼs the matter, oh lady, why are you weeping like this, so inconsolably? What has happened?”
Now the Brahman said, “Tell me, my dear wife, what ails you. If necessary, I shall sell all my properties to remove your sorrow.”
The woman repeated the same words, “Frankly speaking, I do not want to live like this! I donʼt like to live a life like this. Dying is better than living like this!”

The Brahman then took the hands of his wife in his hands and said, crying, “Oh, my dear wife, I can no longer stand your tears. I touch your feet and beseech you, please tell me clearly, why are you crying?”

The woman then started crying louder and said, “I cooked so many items, almost a roomful, in secret, and with equal difficulty I ate them up. I spent hours on end chewing the basella stems, eating the basella pie, páyes, etc. Now that all those things are out of my stomach, I consider this living as no living. I donʼt want to live a life like this! Death is a million times better than this!”
Everyone understood the sorrow of the woman.
The Brahman said, “My dear wife, what you have said is quite true. But, tell us, what can we do about it?”

The kaviráj said, “Please make some room for me; let me try once more.” The kaviráj again unstitched the threads from the stomach of the woman with the help of a bamboo flake. After that, he collected the different food items in pots of different sizes and arranged them in her stomach. After that, he stitched up the stomach again with the medical needle and the thread. After some time, the woman came back to life again. She opened her eyes. She could not control her smile. It looked like a splendid night bathed in the light of a hundred moons, after a long, dark night. Everyone felt very happy. And the Brahman was beside himself with joy.
He told his wife, “My dear wife, I shall treat you with basella everyday. I shall step out of the house only after I see you prepare basella with poppy seeds. Please never cry again.”

From then on, the Brahman and his wife became very close. From then on, the woman gave the Brahman half of whatever cooked. And if the Brahman ever asked for a little more, she would give generously. Sometimes, she would even give away the entire meal to him. Then the Brahman would ask, “Well, my dear wife, have you kept something for yourself?”
The woman would scold with a wry face: “You donʼt have to worry about that; I have made provisions. Please eat whatever I give you.”

Since then, the woman never dined in secret. She ate her birir dál, kuler ambal, nálte-shak, puiṋ-posta and pit́he-páyes, etc. in the presence of everyone. In due course of time, both the Brahman and his wife died. The woman pre-deceased her husband by one hour. So she was not widowed and therefore she did not have to break the shauṋkha [conch-shell bangles].
The chariot came from heaven. The woman asked the charioteer, “Can I take along the necessary items?”
The charioteer said, “I canʼt allow you to take too many things in the chariot. It will make the chariot heavy and this will create a problem when driving.”

So the woman collected some maluk rice [a special kind of rice], basella, rice pie, some salt, oil and spices, sil-norá [mortar and pestle], a portable stove, necessary articles for frying parched rice such as sand, a frying pan, a brush and some special rice for preparing parched rice, a broomstick for sweeping the kitchen, a duster for mopping the stove and some other relevant, important items, and put them in a bag. Then she asked the charioteer, “I want to take along a basketful of sájápán [fully processed betel leaf shaped in the form of a triangle and ready for chewing]. Do you have any objection to it?”
The charioteer said, “No, not a basketful; at the most, you can take some in a small container.”

The woman pressed as many sájápán as she could into a container and put the container in her vanity bag. Then, carrying the vanity bag in one hand and the huge bag on the other, she came out chewing a betel leaf and took her seat in the chariot. The Brahman often suffered from stomach trouble, so he came out sucking some jauṋgii hartuki ( 1 ) [black myrobalan] and wearing a waistbelt. He also put a belt loosely around the waist of his wife because a few days ago, she had had her stomach stitched. The woman mused, “Who knows how long it will take to reach heaven! Anyway, I have taken all the necessary items. Once I reach heaven, I shall start cooking the fine maluk rice and simultaneously prepare alur dam [a variety of highly seasoned thick curry made of potato]. For this reason, I have brought some potatoes from Nainital. I have also brought a tin of dhákái-ciṋŕe [Dhaka variety of beaten rice] as well as nalenguŕ [raw sugar prepared from new date juice] from Jessore. I shall prepare ciṋŕer páyes [porridge of beaten rice]. I have heard that gods take milk. But who knows whether that is cowʼs milk! They are probably supplied with some adulterated milk from a dairy from earth. And why should I bother so much! I have already brought a tin of powdered milk.”

After that, she took out a pán and, while giving it to the Brahman, said, “Look Brahman, you lack grace in everything. Everything of yours is ugly. You should have worn a fine dhoti and a finely frilled (gile kará) páiṋjábi [a loose-fitting upper garment, usually without a collar] made of very fine quality cotton (áddi). Instead, you are just wearing a short, eight-hand long dhoti and a phatuá [a loose, cotton waistcoat]. When people see them, they will only blame me. On such a day of joy, you are just sucking hartuki. Come, take two pieces of cháṋci pán [pure betel leaf]!”

They set out on their voyage. The weather was fine. The sky was cloudless. There was no mechanical snag in the chariot. There was no lack of wind in the sky. The chariot rolled on steadily and it landed at the airport of heaven three minutes before the scheduled time of arrival.
There, the angels came to welcome them.

In ancient times, people used the wood of the sal tree (indrakáśt́ha), marmelos tree (bel kát́h) and fig tree (ud́umbar) as firewood in religious sacrifices. There are several species of ud́umbar or d́umur [fig] of which the common fig and sacrificial fig [Ficus religiosa] are important. It is this sacrificial fig which is called ud́umbar or yájiṋad́umbar. Both these kinds of figs are good for the liver and kidney. They are also medicines for blood pressure. Sacrificial fig is more nutritious and more easily digestible than the common fig.

One meaning of the word ya is sacrificial fig. By and large, the fig is an exception in the world of fruits and flowers. When other flowers bloom or blossom, their inner parts are pushed outside. The fig ( 1 ) is also a flower, but when it blooms it turns inward.

That is why we think that the fig is a fruit; actually, it is a flower. Since it blossoms inside, we call it a fruit, and because we cannot see it bloom, we think that a fig flower is a rare thing which cannot be seen. When someone makes an appearance after a long time, we usually say to that person, “Whatʼs the matter? We donʼt see you at all these days! We wonder if you have turned into a fig flower!” A fig is called d́umar in the Angika language while in most parts of North India it is called gullar.

You must have heard of Phulawariishariif ( 2 ) in Magadha. In those days, Magadha was one of the great centres of Buddhist culture. The whole world looked up to Magadha for wisdom and spiritual wealth (upasampadá). There were many famous Buddhist monasteries in the land of Magadha. In the beginning, these were called Brahmavihár. Later, they came to be known as Baoddhavihár or Buddhist monasteries. Phullarháriibihár was one of the monasteries in Magadha. Phullarháriibihár was later renamed Phulawariishariif. In those days, milk and curd of excellent quality were available in Phullarháriibihár. Cowherds and curd sellers were also to be found in abundance. They were truly skilled in their craft.

Once upon a time, a curd seller was travelling from Phulawariishariif to Ajimabad. On his way, he saw a vast expanse of sandy land along the nearby Ganges River. When he reached there, the tired curd seller sat under a tree to rest. He sat under the tree for quite some time. While resting, he became drowsy. By the way, I forgot to tell you that he did not have weighing instruments – on one side of the pole that he was carrying on his shoulders was a mund of curd and on the other side was a stone with a weight (ojan ( 3 )) of one mund.

The curd seller had thought that on reaching Ajimabad, he would get the stone broken into pieces of different weights – one seer, half seer, one-fourth seer, etc. But when he woke up, the curd seller was greatly surprised to find that his one mund stone had been broken into four pieces, from his curd emanated the fragrance of sandalwood, and the thin film that was on the curd had become four times thicker. At first, even after he reached Ajimabad ( 4 ), he did not realise the significance of the four pieces.

So he started selling the curd, using a spoon as an approximate measure. And, lo and behold, a strange thing happened! It was like the magic box [the earthen container] of Bhanumatii [a famous lady magician from ancient times]. The more curd he sold, the more it grew in quantity, and the film on top became thicker and thicker and thicker! People who came to buy only one seer at once wanted to buy one mund. And those who came to buy one mund wanted to buy ten munds! In one hour, he had sold curd to one lakh [one hundred thousand] inhabitants of Azimabad. The curd seemed to be inexhaustible. Just then, a famous astrologer passed by. When the curd seller saw him, he said,

“Sir, Panditjii [wise man], I have run into a strange problem. See what is happening. The more curd I sell, instead of becoming less, the original quantity becomes more! What strange magic is this! Not only that – while I was sleeping under a tree, my one mund stone spontaneously broke into four pieces.”

The astrologer was stunned. He at once cast the horoscope on a slate and started examining which planets were in, what the stars were, the ráshi [one of the twelve signs of the zodiac] and the lagna [the rising time of any zodiacal sign or the sign of the sunʼs transition to a zodiacal sign] of the tree under which the curd seller had sat, and at which particular point of time of the star and the day of the moon he had got up. After making all these calculations on the interactions of various planets and stars and other factors, he told the curd seller, “Look, you are passing through an excellent time now. Jupiter is auspicious and Saturn is extremely pleased. You should have become a king by now. But by mistake God has written ma in place of ra. As a result, although you have not become a king, you are enjoying good fortune. If you pay the astrologer liberally when giving his fee, he will make this good fortune continue for the rest of your life. In fact, whether you pay more or less, that is up to you. I am not going to ask you nor am I going to say ‘No’ if you pay.”

The curd seller told the astrologer, “Sir, I have just sold three lakh rupees worth of curd. I will pay you one lakh if you can tell me why the stone broke into four pieces and why the curd supply is inexhaustible.”
The astrologer asked, “Did you sit under a fig tree?”
The curd seller answered, “Oh yes, of course. A hundred times yes.”

The astrologer said, “The lid of the container was slightly displaced when a crow stroked it with its beak. Through that gap, a fig dropped into the curd. Since a fig flower fell into it, its supply will never be exhausted. Your curd container will never be depleted. And another fig flower fell on your mund stone, hence the stone broke into four pieces. With the help of those stones as weights, you can sell as many seers of curd as you like at a time. There is no need to sell by approximate weight – you were suffering losses.”

The astrologer continued, “In five minutes, I will conduct a propitiatory ceremony [shánti-svastayan-purascarańa] and make a fig talisman for you. Always wear it on your arm. It will be very beneficial for you. Itʼs not very costly, just about a lakh. You have already made a profit of three lakhs by selling curd. You have given me one lakh as my fees and one lakh for the talisman. And you are still left with one lakh. I shall not take the money even if you want to give it to me. You can buy at least one hundred cows of the best Patna ( 5 ) breed with that money.

When he weighed the four pieces of stone, the curd seller saw that they weighed one seer, three seers, nine seers and twenty-seven seers respectively. With the help of those four pieces, he could sell the exact number of seers that a buyer wanted.
Since then, the glory of the fig has reverberated in the sky and air of entire Magadha.

So now you understand why many beautiful stories about the fig flower are in circulation. The most important point, however, and my last word is – the fig itself is a flower and it does not produce any flower separately. Hence, all these stories are also baseless.

With the pursuit of knowledge and subsequent acquisition of scholarship, human beings learn to exercise control over the mind. They train birds and animals to do various things. A restrained mind is the essence of all kinds of knowledge and learning. Otherwise, one can never learn anything nor can one acquire any knowledge and, even if one acquires knowledge, one cannot retain it. The word ya (by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root yaj) is used for the type of effort by which a human acquires knowledge. It should be borne in mind that, generally, the word ya cannot be used for learning. Only the learning which one tries to acquire for oneʼs own development is called ya. Speaking about development through learning, I am reminded of a story.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: You must have heard about a place called Singur. In very ancient times, Siḿhapur or Siuṋgur was the capital of Ráŕh. Although Singur was not as old as Bardhaman [Burdwan], it was older than most places in Bengal and India. Later, Singur was completely destroyed by the disastrous flooding of the Damodar River. Anyway, there were two rivers – Pulakitá and Ghrtáci – flowing by Siḿhapur. These rivers were the connecting links between Bhagiirathii and Damodar. Close to Siḿhapur, which was situated on the banks of the confluence of these two rivers, was a now-forgotten port called Siḿhalapát́an. It is said that from the port of Siḿhalpát́an, Vijay Singha, the prince of Ráŕh, set off for Siḿhal [Ceylon], and on reaching Siḿhal conquered the country. This is possibly the reason why the port was named Siḿhalpát́an.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: In the course of time, the history of the ancient land of Ráŕh was forgotten, and the people of Ráŕh have also forgotten Siḿhalpát́an. Most of the water belonging to what we now call Hooghly District used to be drained near this port of Siḿhalpát́an. Siḿhapur or Singur, the capital, was situated near Siḿhalpát́an. At one time, Siḿhapur was not only the seat of royal power but also a centre of learning. In Siḿhapur and the surrounding vicinity there lived many great scholars. Today, that Singur is extinct.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: I am talking about the Singur of the medieval period. Singur suffered the same fate as that of other ancient cities. During that time, a pundit started a private school in Singur. From the viewpoint of this 20 century, it is not possible to say anything definite about his scholarship or lack of it, but it is said that in some of the houses in Hooghly District, a tape recording of the punditʼs conversation with a washerwoman can still be found.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: You must have heard of the place called Nasipur. Nasipur existed even during the period of the Pathans. During that age, there lived a rajakinii [washerwoman)] who possessed crores of rupees. She would lie down on gold coins. But she would never spend any money, not even a cowry, let alone a copper coin. She said that to spend one cowry meant to lose one rib. For a long time, the washerwoman had been cooking rice in a leaking pot and had been using a broken hand fan to fan herself. This was how she was happily spending her days. But fate was against her. One day, after washing some rice grains and while pouring them into the pitcher, the pitcher cracked from top to bottom from the impact of the rice. The washerwoman felt sad – not because of the cracked pitcher but because so many rice grains that had spilled on the stove were wasted. More saddening was the fact that the fire on the stove was extinguished by the rice and some rice water had spilled on it. With a very heavy heart, she went to Singur. When she reached there, after much bargaining she purchased a pitcher, a hand fan and a small pot of curd because her granddaughter had been pestering her for curd for quite some time.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: She told the curd seller, “Please give me the residual watery dregs of curd lying in your large pot and donʼt ask any money for it, please.” Thereafter, the washerwoman started walking towards Nasipur with her donkey. On the way, she came across the private school of the pundit we had mentioned earlier. She heard with her own ears the pundit saying, “I have turned so many donkeys into horses, so many horses into humans. Some of them are teaching in colleges, some are writing voluminous books, and I have failed to change you into a horse. Where shall I hide this sorrow?” Then he asked the pupil to kneel down, putting a few pieces of burnt earth under the pupilʼs knees and placing two bricks on his hands. After that, he said, “Remain like that with your tongue out; only then will you learn your lesson.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman could not hold her excitement any longer. She told the Pundit, “Sir, I have five hundred donkeys. For the time being, you take this one at least. First turn it into a horse and then turn it into a human. By selling a horse I can earn more than what I can by selling a donkey and by selling a human ( 1 ), I shall get much more money.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: After paying the money and handing over the donkeys, the washerwoman returned to her house at Nasipur singing film songs all the way. The pundit was beside himself with joy on getting so many donkeys at a time. He sold the donkeys in the market at Hiranpur near Pakur as fast as he could.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The days passed smoothly. One day, all of a sudden, the washerwoman appeared at the school. The pundit said to her, “When your donkeys started reading aikya, vákya, máńikya in the second book, they turned into humans. So I sent some of them to the high school at Tarakeshwar, some to the high school at Baidyabati, some to the high school at Dhanekhali and some to the school at Bhandarhati. After some time, they will finish their education. You can take them back after they pass the M.A. examination.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman could not control her joy. Again, she returned to Nasipur singing classical ragas in new tunes all the way. Ecstatic at the thought of amassing an enormous fortune from selling so many human beings, she took a bellyful of pulse made of pigeon pea, a curry made of potato and poppy seeds and dozed off.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: After a few days, the washerwoman went to the school at Singur again. Her mind was full of hope and her face was radiant with joy. She visualised crores of rupees running after her. Ah! What a joy! She asked the pundit, “Hello, sir, when are you going to return my donkeys? Why donʼt I see them here? Which hell have you sent them to?”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The pundit replied, “No, they have not been sent to any hell. It is a long history. Even the Rámáyańa with its seven parts or the Mahábhárata with its eighteen chapters is no match for their history. All of them are now engaged in different kinds of prestigious jobs. Many of them are teaching in colleges and their fame has travelled far and wide. You tell me, which one of them do you want me to bring to you first?”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman said, “First, I want to bring back home that particular donkey which was especially darkish, a bit longish and which could carry the maximum number of linen bags. I shall sell it for a good price after I make it carry linen bags for a few days.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The Pundit said, “Well, you go to that particular college. There, you will find your donkey teaching English, wearing a suit, complete with trousers, shirt and tie.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman happily left with roasted tobacco between her teeth and a stick in her hand. After some time, she reached her destination. She found that the statement of the Pundit was absolutely correct. A tall Englishman was teaching English in a class; his complexion was slightly dark. The washerwoman easily identified him as the donkey which had been the apple of her eye, her favourite.
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: At that moment, Professor Reverend Banerjee (Bonárjii) was giving a lecture on the dramatic qualities of Shakespeare. The washerwoman saw him from a distance and realised that she had come to the right place. Now, she must come to the notice of the donkey. Thus, she selected a spot on the verandah just outside the door of the classroom from where she could see the jewel of a donkey and from where the donkey could also see her. The washerwoman thought, “There stands my favourite donkey and it carried so many bags of linen in my house for so long. It will recognise me as soon as it sees me. It will come out braying in joy.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: But, alas, Reverend Banerjee did not look that way at all. He continued his lecture in English in British style. The washerwoman noticed that his facial movements were very much like her donkeyʼs. The shivering of the voice and the movement of the lips were almost identical. The washerwoman felt very sad. The donkey was so close to her and yet it failed to recognise her. The washerwoman started moving the stick in her hand, sometimes pushing it forward, sometimes drawing it back and articulating at the same time, “áy áy áy á á á … áy áy áy ….” Even then, the professor did not look in her direction. The washerwoman raised her voice a little higher and said, “á á á, tu tu tu, á á á, tu tu tu.” Still, the professor did not cast a glance at her. The washerwoman raised her voice even higher and said, “Tu tu tu, kur kur kur, hyáddá hyáddá hyáddá, hidde hidde hidde, tu tu tu, kur kur kur, hyáddá hyáddá hyáddá, hidde hidde hidde.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman kept on changing her forms of address, but it was of no avail. Finally, when she had run out of ways to get the donkeyʼs attention, she said, “What audacity! Now turned into a human with a suit, and you canʼt recognise me! Wait and see the fun! I shall flay the skin off your back with my stick. Pretending to be ignorant! Your name was kelo gádhá [black donkey] and now you have become rebáreṋŕi pepecor Bonárjii [Reverend Professor Banerjee].”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The professor left the class and came rushing to her. He thought that the person was probably mentally deranged. He said in English-accented Bengali, “T́umi ki baliit́echo madam, ámi bujhit́e páritechi ná. T́umi keno ciitkár karit́echo.” [“I donʼt understand, madam. What you are saying? Why are you shouting?”]
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman replied, “Donʼt try to fool me. You are a donkey. Now, after being educated, you have become a human. Now you are sporting English. What strange fashions you are displaying here while the bags of linen have piled up into a hill at home! How long am I going to push the cart? Come home with me. I will make you labour intensely, putting bags of linen on your back right from today. Enough of your lecturing!”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: Reverend Banerjee was nonplussed. The students rushed to his aid. They asked the washerwoman, “We canʼt make out what you are trying to say.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman replied, “This is my donkey which I had sent to school for its education. After being educated, it has become a human and now it cannot recognise me.” The washerwoman put her hand on her forehead and started lamenting, “Alas, what has befallen me! Why in the world did I send it to be educated!”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The students said, “Aunty, you are making a mistake. He was never a donkey. He is a human, alive and kicking, a great scholar. He has written notes which would weigh three to four hundred metric tons, and one cannot pass an examination without reading them. You have come to the wrong place, aunty; for sure you have come to the wrong place. Recently, he has done historical research. In one of his recent books, he has established that Aurangzeb was not a descendant of Akbar; he was actually Akbarʼs grandfather. Yesterday, he has just completed another research paper. His point was that people took Sita as the wife of Rama, but actually, Sita was Ramaʼs paternal aunt. Why do you call such a profound scholar a donkey?”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman said, “Look, I am not talking about the present. I admit he has become a human and a great scholar. I am talking about the past when he was a donkey.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The students said, “We donʼt know anything about the past. But we have heard that he is a pure Englishman.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman replied, “If he really is a pure Englishman, why does he use the word Báṋŕujje as his surname?”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The students said, “Oh, no, no, no, no, why should he write Báṋŕujje? Had he been a Bengalee, he would have written Báńdhyopadhyay; had he been half-English, he would have written Banerjii. But since he is a pure Englishman, he writes Bonárji. Those ignorant people do not even know his real name. His real name is Byágár Byáhán Bonárji. In short, B.B. Bonárji. We have come across many such foolish people who by mistake pronounce his name Byághraváhana Báṋŕujje. But he has never accepted that name. Besides, he is a pure Englishman. His name cannot be Báṋŕujje, nor can it be Byághraváhana.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The washerwoman said, “But his complexion is very much like my donkeyʼs. If he were really a pure Englishman, his complexion would be bright red.”
chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

t: The students said, “Oh, no. He is a one hundred percent pure Englishman. He was on his way to this country on a plane, when suddenly he fell out of the window like a ripe mango. And look where he fell! Into the fathomless waters of the Black Sea. For one hour, he swam in different styles: sometimes going underwater and sometimes using back strokes. After one hour, he reached the shore uninjured except that his complexion had turned black. If one remains in the water of the Black Sea for such a long time, can one avoid turning black? Since his arrival here, he has been washing his face with soap three hundred times every day and using many other cosmetics to regain his original complexion. Once it so happened that because of intense rubbing, the skin on his face peeled off. Since then, he has stopped trying to regain his original complexion. He said, 'Since I now live in the country of black people, it is better to look black. A black human is also a human. In fact, the brilliance of learning makes the black complexion more glittering.”

chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

chapterTitle: Beating a Donkey into A Man

See, somehow, I have been made to perform so much penance. I have had a hard enough lesson!”
