t: When something comes in contact with fire, there can be three kinds of reactions: you can burn an object, ignite an object or singe an object. Fire can be used for burning, igniting or singeing. It can also be used for baking.

When we burn an object, the exterior is destroyed by fire, but the interior becomes soft with the heat of the fire. When we ignite an object, both the interior and exterior are destroyed by contact with the fire and are turned into ashes. We burn a brinjal. We ignite the wick of a lamp. When the exterior of an object becomes more or less burnt while the interior does not become very soft but is only slightly affected, we call it singeing. For singeing (jhalsáno), the word ra is applied by adding the suffix d́a to the verbal root rá.

When an object undergoes a certain change from contact with heat, but no part of it is burnt, we call it baking. The word ra cannot mean baking and that is why we cannot describe baked bread as ra. How do you say it then? Burning a brinjal, igniting a brinjal or singeing a brinjal? Certainly you say ‘burning a brinjal’ because after burning the brinjal, you eat the kernel.
Speaking of brinjal burning, I recall an anecdote.

In the old days, plays were often very melodramatic. The dialogue of a drama should be natural but it is slightly different from the normal conversations of mundane everyday life. In daily life, when we talk among ourselves, we do not want anyone else to hear us, nor do we think of compelling others to hear us. We confine the conversation to ourselves. But in a dramatic dialogue, the actors have to bear in mind that the audience or spectators should be able to hear what they are saying and should understand from their gestures themselves what they want to say. This is the main difference between normal conversations and dramatic dialogues. Of course, there are other differences as well.

In those days, most dramas were melodramas. Once, a famous opera troupe came from Kolkata to our village. I went to watch the performance along with my grandmother (the expression in those days was “to go and listen to operatic songs”). The king was in a dialogue with his queen. The king, with his tin foil robe, tin foil crown and tin foil-wrapped weapon, was getting ready to go to the battlefield with much fanfare. At that moment, the king and queen were conversing in a melodramatic fashion. The queen was saying, “Paráńeshvar, práńanátha! Kotha yáo pheliyá ámáre?” [“Oh, heart of my life, Oh, Lord of my life, where are you going, leaving me behind?”]
My granny remarked, “What drivel! See the affectation of that woman!”
It was also not to my liking at all. The queen shouted for the second time in a deep, rumbling voice (heṋŕe galá) ( 1 ), “Paráńeshvar, práńanátha!”
I could not stand it any longer. I said, “Begun-poŕá mákho bhát.” [Mix rice with burnt brinjal.]
My granny was delighted to hear it and commended, “Well said, very well said. I shall make you a diamond-studded ring.”
Anyway, burnt brinjal is a food item. So we say begun-poŕá [burnt brinjal] and not bagun jváláno [ignited brinjal].

The verbal root ruś means not bursting out in anger, to suppress anger. Bursting out in anger is called krodha. But when anger is suppressed, we call it roś. Krodha can be understood immediately, but it takes time to understand roś. Suppose somebody was angry with you and subsequently everything became normal and you have probably forgotten about the incident. Suppose, after quite some time, you invite that person to dinner and he replies harshly, “Iʼm not eating today.” You then realise that he has suppressed anger in his mind. This is called roś.

Suppose your boss at your workplace is angry with you but she does not let you know. You have to work with her very carefully and are almost constantly engaged in a battle of wits with her. Suppose the headmaster of the school is very angry with you but because it is suppressed anger, he does not show it. Suppose you have to take part in the wedding entourage of your friendʼs marriage. You apply for leave and the headmaster of the school does not grant you leave. He says, “There is tremendous pressure of work now and two teachers are suffering from influenza. So, in spite of my best intentions, I canʼt grant you leave now.” You see through the game but you canʼt do anything. So you decide to fight an intellectual battle. You now write an application:
“My mother is seriously ill. Her condition is critical. Therefore, please grant me three daysʼ leave.”

The headmaster is compelled to grant you leave on account of your intelligent move. And so, you join the wedding entourage of your friend wearing a fine and frilled dress (gile kará páiṋjábi) and attend his marriage ceremony. Now, you have learnt how to handle roś. The word ra is used for roś. And, again, the word ra can also be used for one who nurses roś.
Speaking about the application for leave, I am reminded of a story from the British period.

Do you know Káliikrpá Bhat́cáj [Kalikripa Bhattacharya] of Shantipur? But how could you know? It happened such a long time ago. It was during the British period. Kálii Bhat́cáj was employed in the civil service in Kashii [Benaras], drawing a fat salary. In those days, anybody who had some knowledge of English could easily get a job. It is said that in those days, the life of a particular class of people consisted of four forms. The first form was for admission to an English medium school. The second form was to obtain a certificate from the school after learning elementary English. The third form was the application form to join the railway service. The fourth form was the platform where one would stand with a railway flag in hand. Kálii Bhat́cháj was much better than these people. Previously, when he was the station master of Railways, he spoke English fluently.

Once, a serious accident took place when a running mail train collided with a stationary goods train at the station. The red-faced, big Englishmen came from Delhi to conduct an enquiry. Kálii Bhat́cáj did not feel in the least scared. But in order to evoke their pity and to apprise them of his poverty, he said, “I, poor man sir, even then forty leaves [forty plates made of leaves] fall daily in my house sir. See my condition, sir. I am a poor man, sir. Even then I have to feed forty people daily. Please understand my situation, sir.”

The Englishmen thought that Kálii Bhat́cháj was probably nervous. So in order to reassure him, they said, “There is nothing to be nervous about. You just tell us whatever you have to say. You can speak in Bengali because we have an interpreter with us.”

I have already told you that Kálii Bhat́cáj spoke English fluently. So why should he speak in Bengali? He said, “Málgáŕii standing sir, melgáŕii coming sir. I red flag sir. My assistant station master red sir. My signaller red, my worker red. All were red́e – red́e – red. I said pai pai not come, not come. Even then train ghyáccáḿ.” [“The goods train was standing at the station. The mail train was coming very fast. I showed the red flag. My assistant station master, my signaller and my attendant – all of us showed the red flags – the platform was full of red. I shouted repeatedly, ‘Please donʼt come, donʼt come, donʼt comeʼ. Even then, the mail train came speeding and rammed into the goods train.”]
The Englishmen reported that Kálii Bhat́cháj was innocent and that a man with such an excellent knowledge of English was a precious asset to the British Government.
They recommended that instead of keeping him in the Railways, he be nominated an I.C.S. ( 1 )

At that time, Kálii Bhat́cáj was in Kashii. A grandfather also has a grandfather. So there was also someone who could overrule Kálii Bhat́cáj. For so long, Kálii Bhatcáj had been spending his days quite happily and peacefully. Whenever necessary, he would be absent for eight to ten days from the office without obtaining any leave. Sometimes, he would simply hang his coat on the chair and go home. He instructed the attendant, “If the boss comes, just tell him that I have gone to the bathroom. And in the meantime, you call me at my home.” Kálii Bhat́cájʼs senior officials who came to visit him were all red-faced Englishmen. So he had no difficulty going on leave because those Englishmen were not familiar with the customs and conventions of this country. Whatever Kálii Bhat́cáj told them, they took it as gospel truth. But life does not always flow smoothly. Finally, an Indian became Kálii Bhat́cájʼs boss. He knew all the local customs. Once, on coming to enquire about Kálii Bhat́cáj, he found him absent from the office. On asking the Establishment Clerk, he came to know that there was no application for leave from Kálii Bhat́cáj. He then issued a ‘show cause chargesheet’ against Kálii Bhat́cáj.

In the following three days, nothing happened. During those three days, Kálii Bhat́cájʼs beard had grown a little. Kálii Bhat́cáj came to the office barefoot. Needless to say, he had heard the rumour about the chargesheet but did not know the details. As soon as he reached the office, the Establishment Clerk narrated everything to him. When everyone saw Kálii Bhat́cájʼs mahágurunipátdashá ( 2 ) [formal mourning signs with unshaven beard and bare feet] on the death of his parent, they understood why Kálii Bhat́cáj had been absent from the office. After hearing what the Establishment Clerk had to say, Kálii Bhat́cáj gave a wry smile on his emaciated face and remarked, “How can I blame my boss? He does not know about my misfortune.”
Kálii Bhat́cáj wrote an application immediately. It ran as follows:
Sir,

With due respect, I, your humble servant, would like to state that I belong to a family of high caste (kuliin) Brahman of Shantipur. My grandfather, the late Shataratha Bhattacarya, had one hundred wives. ( 3 ) Every third day, my grandfather would go to one of his wives to collect obeisance money. Thus he spent three hundred days. For the remaining sixty-five days, he stayed at home and examined the account of the proceeds from the obeisances and looked after the farm. My grandfather died long ago. My grandmothers are also following suit singly or in twos. Three died last year and this year, five have already passed away. Possibly because it is colder this year, they are dying in greater numbers. However, sir, I have stated the truth. Up till now, twenty-two grandmothers have gone to heaven (with a remaining seventy-eight grandmothers yet to die).”

Thanks to his application, Kálii Bhat́cáj escaped that time. Kálii Bhatcáj had enormous suppressed anger or roś against this boss. He took revenge against this boss by the exercise of his intellect. Of course, he had to move about in mourning dress for a few days. The word ra is used for such suppressed anger or roś.

In Sanskrit, the verbal root ras means to call by creating a special type of sound; second, to flow; and third, to be sticky. Suppose you are here and on the other side of the vast field stands Khudua Mahato. How would you call him? You will shout, “Oh, Khudua Mahato … ohhhhhhhhh....” To be carried means to flow, to move slightly like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. The third meaning is to feel sticky. For example, glue or mango gum. In all three cases we obtain the word rasa from the verbal root ras. Because of the presence of this juice or rasa, a particular kind of sweet is called rasagollá [round-shaped juicy sweet made of fresh cheese]. There are other such sweets – rasamálái and rasabaŕá.

Fowlers use the stickiness of glue to catch birds in the forest by spreading different kinds of glue. They keep mango gum in a comparatively large pot and scatter a few grains of paddy on it for the birds. Sometimes, they even throw a few ucciḿŕes [an insect similar to the cricket] on that gum. When the birds come to eat the paddy or ucciḿŕes, their legs get stuck in the glue. Then the fowlers come and catch them one by one.

Once, I had told you the story of Phatu. I told you how he caught a few jackals by keeping mango gum on a mat made of kusha grass. Now I remember another story where an intelligent human caught hold of a ghost with the help of mango gum. If you want to hear the story, then here it is.

Kyáblákánta Kaiṋjilál was a famous man from Kadamtala (Chinsura). There was no record in his diary that he ever gave anything to anybody. But he never hesitated to ask for things. Living in affluence, he would always grumble about his poverty – as is the wont of successful merchants. Even when they made a profit of crores of rupees, they would always grumble that the market was down.

One day, Kyáblákánta thought of keeping all his money intact by taking up the “style of a python”. Perhaps you know what is the “pythonʼs style”. Keeping its mouth wide open, it moves very fast so that all kinds of animals and insects enter straight into its stomach. When its stomach is fully gorged, it shuts its mouth and then hibernates for one week, sometimes for a fortnight if necessary. After the food is digested, it starts to move again. Humans are said to adopt the python style when they move about with the intention to take whatever comes their way.

Kyábalákánta set off in python style. After he had gone a short distance along G.T. Road [Grand Trunk Road], he met an angel of divine lustre. When he saw the angel, he said, “Hello, my friend, it is evident that you are an embodiment of kindness and you understand the joys and sorrows of human beings. You give away your food to feed one who is hungry. I feel a great respect for you. I have not eaten anything yet. You have probably appeared before me because you know this.”

The angel said, “Ah, ha, ha, ha! You should have told me before that you are hungry.” He then opened the mouth of his magic bag, cast a glance at the ripe mangoes of a wayside tree and said, “Let those ripe mangoes come into this bag.” At once, the mangoes came jumping and hopping and entered the plastic bag in the hand of the angel.
The angel said, “Kyáblákánta, please eat these mangoes. We shall resume our journey when your stomach is full.”
Kyáblákánta eagerly ate up all the mangoes and then said, “Alas, there has been a great mistake. I have not asked you whether you have had your food.”
The angel replied, “Today is the eleventh day of the moon [fasting day].”

From that very moment, Kyáblákántaʼs greedy eyes were on the plastic bag. Kyáblákánta and the angel walked on and on, but the road did not seem to have an end. Kyáblá was not worried about food because the plastic magic bag of the angel was with them. They reached a particular spot where members of a poor family were crying bitterly. The angel stopped.
Kyáblákánta asked, “Why are you stopping here? Canʼt you see that they are lamenting importunately? When they see us, they will immediately intensify their lamentation.”
The angel said, “But we must find out what happened. Once we know the cause of their sorrow, we can probably remove it as well.”

After talking to them, the angel learnt that their only son was critically ill; the doctor had given up hope. The angel prescribed some medicines and the boy came round at once. The family stopped crying and repeatedly expressed their gratitude to the angel. They said, “What can we give you? Please take this goat.”
The angel replied, “No, thank you. Medical treatment is not my profession. When I saw your grief, I felt for you. And since I knew the remedy, I administered it.”
Kyáblá said, “Please, please take the goat. Who knows, it may be of some use in the future.”
The angel said, “Well, you are so keen to take it, but who will carry it? Can it walk such a long distance with us like a human?”
Kyáblá replied, “Donʼt worry about that. I will carry it on my shoulders.”

The angel and Kyáblákánta continued their journey. After some time, they came to a royal mansion. They heard wailing from the royal mansion. The princess was on the brink of death. The king was crying. The queen was crying. But all their wailing was surpassed by the wailing of the ministers and government officers who were profusely shedding crocodile tears.
The angel asked, “Whatʼs the matter? What has happened?”
They cried, “Look! The princess is critically ill; she may die any moment! Can you do something about it?”
The angel said, “Unfortunately, I donʼt have any resources except sincere solicitude. So I offer my best wishes to the princess.”

The princess started to recover. The king and the queen were very happy. They wanted to present one metric ton of precious stones – diamonds, sapphires, pearls, etc. to the angel. The angel said, “What shall I do with them? I have not brought these things to earth and I shall not carry them back either.”
Kyáblá said, “Please, please give them to me. Let me keep them. Who knows, they may be of some use in the future.”
The angel said, “But let me make it very clear that I wonʼt be able to carry them.”
Kyáblá replied, “I shall carry them.”

Kyáblá then put that huge load of precious stones plus the goat on his shoulders and continued walking. He felt intense agony due to the heavy burden. It was so heavy that he could not even walk properly. Despite this, he continued walking, keeping pace with the angel. After some time, they reached the bank of a river.
Kyáblá said, “Let us slaughter the goat here and eat rice and meat.”
The angel said, “I donʼt have any appetite. Iʼd rather go and have a dip in the river. Wonʼt you go for a bath?”
Kyáblá said, “I feel out of sorts. So I shall skip a bath today.”

The angel went for his bath. Kyáblá started cooking rice and meat. After he had finished cooking, Kyáblá sat and waited for the angel. But the angel was nowhere in sight. Kyábláʼs mouth began to water and he became very impatient. Unable to control himself any longer, he ate up the spleen, liver and heart [kalejá ( 1 )] of the goat. Just as Kyáblá finished, the angel returned, smiling.
Kyáblá said, “My friend, you are very late. The meat and rice are getting cold.“ The angel replied, ”I have already told you that I donʼt have any appetite. You should have taken your meal.”
Kyáblá said, “How can that be possible? How can we have differing privileges during the same journey? Is it possible that I eat when you are not eating?”
The angel said, “Then you do one thing. Give me the spleen, liver and heart of the goat, and you have the rest.”

Kyáblákánta pretended to search for the spleen, liver and heart by fingering through the pieces. After searching for a long time, Kyayblá told the angel, “Look, my friend, I canʼt find the pieces that you want to eat. I have no knowledge of biology, but I have a feeling that a goat does not have any liver, spleen or heart.”
The angel said, “So what can you do? You had better finish the meat and rice. Meanwhile, let me say my prayers.”

This was exactly what Kyáblá wanted. He finished his elaborate lunch and then said, “Look here, my friend, let us share between us the huge load of precious stones that I am carrying. You make the division.”
The angel said, “Oh no, itʼs better that you divide the stones.”

Kyáblá thought, “If I keep the angel in good humour, I shall have greater chance of getting more wealth in the future.” He said, “It would be better if this division were done by a wise and intelligent person. So I request you to divide the stones.”
The angel said, “Well, since you insist, let me do the dividing.” The angel divided the entire wealth of precious stones into three equal parts.
Kyáblá asked, “There are only two of us. Why did you divide them into three parts?”
The angel said, “Well, one part is for you, one part is for me and the third part is for the person who ate the liver, spleen and heart of the goat.”
Kyáblá shouted with joy, “It was I who ate the liver, spleen and heart of the goat! So that part is also for me!”
The angel said, “Why that part only? You take all the wealth. I donʼt need it. And since you are a liar, I leave your company right now.”
Kyáblá thought, “What should I do next? What I have obtained is no small thing. Now, if I can get his plastic bag, my profit will be complete.”

Kyáblá then played a ruse. He bought two ready-to-eat betel leaves from a nearby shop, gave them to the angel and said, “My friend, I really cannot bid you farewell empty-handed. So I request you to please keep these two betel leaves as a memento from a poor man.”

An angel does not chew betel leaves. Even then, for the sake of courtesy, he accepted them. The angel started to walk away. Kyáblá saw that the angel had forgotten to return his courtesy. He quickly said to him, “My friend, wonʼt you give me a memento?”
The angel said, “Do I have anything at all to give you? Whatever wealth I had, I have already given them all to you. What do I have now?”
Kyáblákánta said, “If you really donʼt have anything, then at least give me that plastic bag.”
The angel said, “All right then, take it.”

The angel then went his way. Kyáblákánta went another way. Kyáblákánta continued walking and walking, whichever which way came into view, “Pathik ámi pathei básá /ámár yeman yáoá teman ásá [I am a traveller and my dwelling is on the path, and I come the way I go]. He passed one field after another; nothing else came within his sight. Kyáblákánta with the heavy bag of wealth on his shoulders tottered onwards. The goat was bleating in his stomach, creating a serious problem. He must reach some shelter before dark. By and by, a town appeared. After going some distance, he saw a huge house with a flower garden in front and a fruit garden at the back. But how could it be? Such a big house and not a single light was on! It looked as if there was nobody in the house. He stopped in front of the gate. He stood there for a long time. Finally, a government servant came and asked him why he was standing there like that.
Kyáblá said, “I need a shelter only for tonight. I wish to get permission to spend the night in this house.”

The government servant said, “Look, I am the caretaker of the house. You can stay here with my permission. But the particularity of this house is that during the day, there is no problem staying in it; once night falls, there is danger. As soon as the sun goes down, ghosts appear and they make life hell for the guest with their various dances and songs. Occasionally, in the past some high-ranking government officers and ministers sought permission to stay here in order to enjoy film songs and cabaret dances. I granted them permission. But at the last moment, they cancelled their stay out of fear that female spirits would break their necks. Since then, the king has made a rule that if anybody wants to spend a night in this house, he must sign a risk bond – that in the event of his death he himself will be responsible but if by good luck he survives – then the king will not only give him half the kingdom but also his daughter in marriage if the horoscopes and other conditions are found suitable.”

Kyáblákánta at once signed the risk bond. He inspected every room and found that every room was properly furnished with a bedstead and other furniture. There were attached toilets and bathrooms as well – all immaculate. The air conditioner was also functioning properly. The carpets were all new and brushed clean. He selected the room facing the south on the first floor because it is said that the south-facing room is the most comfortable. It is said:
Purve háṋs pashime Báṋsh,
Uttar beŕe dakśiń cheŕe.

It means: On the eastern side of the house there should be ducks; that is, a pond or a tank. On the west side there should be bamboo groves. On the north side there should be a boundary wall, otherwise in winter the chilling Himalayan winds will make the room terribly cold. And the south should be left open for the soothing effect of the gentle evening breeze from the Bay of Bengal.

Well, I forgot to tell you that just after the angel left, Kyáblákánta passed through the historically famous village of Janai in the district of Hooghly. There, he had collected some specialty sweets – khaicuŕ and monohará – and had put them in his plastic bag. When he entered the mansion, the first thing he did was to consume them. Then he lay down on the milk-white bed.
Some time passed quite comfortably. After more time had elapsed, he felt drowsy and heard several ghosts singing in a deep, rumbling voice close to his ears:
Dhinṋ tá dhináṋ paṋcá nonáṋ
Háṋŕ bháṋte bháṋt caŕiyeṋ deṋná.
[Oh, how much joy, we have enjoyed rotten custard apple, now, cook some bones and rice in a pitcher.]
Kyáblákánta felt very annoyed, gave a few slaps to the ghosts and then turned over on the bed. After some time, he heard a few female ghosts by his side singing film songs:
Meṋronṋá meṋronṋá moṋdeṋer meṋronṋá,
Máṋriṋileo moṋrá eṋ ghar cháṋŕibaṋná.
[Please donʼt beat us, please donʼt beat us.
Even if you beat us, we wonʼt leave the room.]

Kyáblákánta thought, “I have the sure-fire remedy with which to tackle them. If, looking at the ghosts, both male and female, I say just once, 'Let all these male and female ghosts come into this bagʼ, then they will be compelled to enter the bag.” Then it dawned on him that the rule was that while saying the command, he must look at the person whom he wants to go inside the bag. But the ghosts, both male and female, were phantoms. They were not visible. One could hear their dances and songs, one could touch them, one could beat them, but because they were spirits, they could not be seen with oneʼs eyes. Kyáblákánta wondered what to do about it. If he were to try and catch them or tie them up, they would fly away through the window of the first floor. “What can be done?” he mused. “What, really, can be done?”

A few days ago, he had read the story of Phatu. In that story, Phatuʼs mother had put mango glue on a mat of kusha grass for the jackals to sit. As a result, the jackals could not run away. He thought, “Suppose I do that.”

Kyáblá hurriedly left the room and went downstairs. At the back of the house, there was a huge mango tree of the madhukulakulii variety. Kyáblá quickly took a katári [iron cutting weapon] and cut off a part of its bark.
The tree asked, “Kyáblá, how much glue do you need?”
Kyáblá replied, “I presume they would be about 700 or 800 strong.”
The tree said, “I think you are talking about the ghosts.”
Kyáblá said, “Thatʼs right.”
The tree said, “The male and female ghosts together with their children number 12345. I will give you sufficient glue. You take it along with you.”

Kyáblákántaʼs joy knew no bounds. He returned to his room with the glue and pasted it thoroughly on the carpet. Then he lay down with a leg on the side pillow, a cheek on the cheek pillow and his head on the head pillow. He did not fall asleep immediately. It was that time when the goddess of sleep was waiting outside and in two minds as to whether to enter the room or not. Suddenly, the ghosts began beating their drums and the female ghosts started their cabaret dance in the middle of the room.

Kyáblá concluded from the noises he heard that they were dancing. After dancing for some time, the female ghosts were unable to lift their legs. They said to one another, “My dear, why arenʼt you dancing? What has happened to your feet?”
Another said, “What has happened to your leg? Why canʼt you raise your leg? Why?”

Then all of them shouted in a chorus [in their usual nasalized voice], “Our legs are getting stuck to something. We do not know what. Oh, Kyáṋbláṋdáṋdáṋ, what have you done? Does a gentleman behave like this?”
The male ghosts also shouted, “Our feet are stuck as well! Oh, Kyábládádá, is this what you had in mind? It would have been better if you had beaten us with a heavy hammer.”
The female ghosts said, “It would have been better if you had shaved our heads clean.”

The moment the ghosts tried to use their hands to untie their legs, their hands also became stuck in the glue and could not be lifted. They started lamenting, “Has such danger ever befallen a person! We have committed sins in many of our births and therefore have become stuck in the mango glue.”

Kyáblákánta then tied each of the ghosts with a strong nylon cord. He also tied their hands behind their backs. One could not see the ghosts but one could see the nylon cords with which they were tied. So now, he opened the mouth of the plastic bag and commanded, “Let all the ghosts who have been tied with this nylon cord enter this bag.”

There was no escape – all the ghosts obediently entered the bag. On that day, they were 750 in number; Kyáblákánta himself had counted them. Then he closed the mouth of the plastic bag with a very strong cord and put it under his bed. After that, sitting on his bed, he contemplated for some time and then lay down.

All the while, the ghosts were imploring loudly from the bag, “Oh Kyábládádá, we touch your feet, we prostrate ourselves before you. Please save us. How can you be so cruel? You are forcing as many as 750 people to die of suffocation, crowding us into a small bag. This is a tragedy, a Black Hole ( 2 ) slaughter! Are you completely devoid of any compassion? We prostrate ourselves before you; please let us off.”

Without paying any heed to their pleas, Kyáblákánta went to sleep snoring nicely. The following morning, his first task was to take the bag to a smithy. On reaching the workshop, he told the blacksmith, “Please take this money. Oh, my dear blacksmith, take it and hammer on the bag as much as you can. Use the huge hammer of a blacksmith and not the small hammer of a goldsmith.” The blacksmith started hammering heavily and still more heavily, making different kinds of loud sounds.

All the ghosts, both male and female, started wailing from within the plastic bag, “Oh, we are undone! Oh, we are dying! We shall never misbehave like that again. We shall never sing film songs. We shall never dance cabaret. We shall never give trouble to any gentleman. We admit our mistakes. Please let us off!”
But who was listening to them? The blacksmith continued hammering on the bag.

After some time there was complete silence. It was obvious that the ghosts had given up the ghost! But do you want to know what exactly happened? Seven hundred and forty-nine ghosts were hammered to death by the blacksmith; but, one ghost was still alive. He was very clever. He thought, “This hammering will go on as long as I continue to cry in pain. Better that I keep silent. Then they will think that I am dead and they will stop hammering.”

That was precisely what happened. When the noises made by the ghosts had completely stopped and Kyáblákánta was about to shake the bones out of the bag after untying the strong cord, the surviving ghost dashed out and, while flying towards the sky, warned Kyáblákánta, “Kyáblá, I have taken note of you. Remember, time does not pass in a constant way. Today, it is your time; but my time will also come.”

Kyáblákánta then collected the bones of the other ghosts and went to the funeral ground, reciting the mourning slogan, “Bala Hari” [Say Hari]. There, he properly performed the obsequies with the help of a Brahman, a specialist in the ritual of cremating dead bodies. Thereafter he offered the bones to the water. Ten days later, he elaborately performed three kinds of sháddha ceremony [obsequies] – dánságar [liberal gifts], brśotsarga [offering an ox] and śoŕasha [offering sixteen items] so that the spirits would get salvation. Then he went to the king and demanded half the kingdom. The king not only gave him half the kingdom but also his daughter in marriage, after taking into consideration the caste, clan, horoscope, etc.

A long time passed. Kyáblákánta thought, “This world is transitory. Let me now go in search of something permanent. He set off with the hope of reaching heaven. He walked almost unceasingly. After travelling some distance, he saw a fork on the road, which meant that he had come to a junction where three roads converged.

Kyáblákánta started thinking. All kinds of thoughts crowded in his mind. He had heard that there were different ways: one, shreya [beneficial] and the other, preya [desirable]. He had heard from the angel that artha [material gain] and paramártha [spiritual gain] were two different paths. He thought, “These two paths before me – are they also like that? What shall I do? Which path should I take? Whom should I consult?”

Around that time, he noticed a handsome ascetic giving away his only blanket to a poor man and wrapping him with it. Kyáblá thought, “Let me ask him which path I should take.” He asked the ascetic, “Father, I want to go to heaven; please tell me which path I should take.”

The ascetic replied, “The narrow path that you see in front of you, so full of thorns and rough stones with many ups and downs, is the path that will take you to heaven after six years. But by then, after several falls on the rough stones, you will be seriously injured. Your hands and legs will be torn by thorns on the road. The ghosts, both male and female, standing on either side of the road will constantly discourage you. It is a very hard journey, no doubt, but this is the path to the Good. Honest men choose this path.”
The ascetic did not tell Kyáblákánta anything about the other path. Kyáblákánta therefore enquired, “Well, Father, why didnʼt you say anything about this wide, excellent road?”

The ascetic replied, “Well, the road that you are looking at – you see how wide it is, how nicely pitched, how smooth, how it is even more comfortable than a rich manʼs bed? It is a road on which you can comfortably lie on a summer night and and where you can happily bask in the sun at winter noon. There are macadamised footpaths on either side. You are not likely to get hurt even if you fall, teetering and vomiting, after drinking a lot of wine. It is a road on which if you walk fast for a few days, you will quickly reach the huge gate of hell. The male and female ghosts that you meet on the way will only encourage you to move along.”

After the ascetic had left, Kyáblákánta mused, “Six daysʼ journey along this paved road is much more comfortable than six yearsʼ troublesome journey along the road to the Good, even though it is the desirable path. Let me try this road first.”

In the course of his journey, Kyáblákánta noticed a strange thing. The road had a downward slope. The more he walked, the more comfortable became the journey. Not only the ghosts on either side of the road, but also his forgotten friends and relatives were telling him, “You have done the best thing, the right thing. Walk faster. This road to hell is the road of the intelligent and the intellectuals. Eat whatever you like; donʼt be choosy. We also ate according to our inclinations. As a result, some of us died of cholera and some of diabetes. Even after coming here, we have been eating whatever we feel like. We have indulged unrestrainedly in intoxicants and we have died of liver cirrhosis. After arriving here, we are continuing the same practice. This is known as the path of pleasure. Here, the custom is: eat, drink and be merry, for life is short. We are happy to see you. As soon as you reach hell, we shall make you a member of our infernal club.”

The more Kyáblákánta advanced, the faster became his speed. Consequently, he reached the gate of hell well before the expected time of arrival. As he approached the gate, he saw that the ghost who had somehow escaped with broken bones from the smithy was working here as head of the security department. Recently, the plasters had been removed from different parts of his body but his neck and mouth had become crooked. When he saw Kyáblá, he motioned his assistants to go forward to welcome him with a garland of cowdung cakes. The ghost told Kyáblákánta, “In the smithy, you gave me a beating with the hammer. I told you then that I, too, shall have my chance. Now, you are in my clutches. I have apprised the king of hell [Yamarája] of your antecedents in full. Come, come inside, then you will see how I shall bring you to book.”
Kyáblákánta sensed danger. He thought, “If I enter through the gate, I wonʼt be able to come out.” So he told the ghost, “Please wait for a while. I shall come back shortly.”

Kyáblákánta mused, “It is better to undertake six yearsʼ hazardous journey than to suffer ad infinitum the tortures inflicted by this ghost in hell. There, at least, I wonʼt suffer the agony of torture.”

Kyáblákánta started walking in the opposite direction. As he began to walk, he noticed to his dismay that the road which was sloping downwards enabling him to practically glide down in very little time now had an upward slope, making it painful for him to walk, and his knees ached as a result. All the male and female ghosts, familiar and strange, standing on either side of the road started threatening him, and some were preparing to beat him. They said, “You naughty boy, you have become senile. Thatʼs why you want to walk along this pebbled road full of thorns and shrubs and sharp stones, instead of taking the beautiful macadamized, paved road.” Some of them then rushed to beat him with a long piece of wood.

But Kyáblákánta remained firm in his decision. He told all of them, “Whether you kill me or cut me to pieces, I wonʼt listen to you. That road is not meant for me. I am going back to the junction where the three roads converged.”

After a very tiresome journey of fifteen to twenty days, he finally reached the junction where the three roads converged. Although he was very tired and exhausted on account of the tedium of the journey, he felt a tremendous sense of comfort, joy, and gave a sigh of great relief at the prospect of an expansive life. Now, on reaching the crossing, he took the narrow path full of shrubs, bushes, thorns and innumerable sharp stones scattered all about. Many male and female ghosts as well as many familiar and unfamiliar faces had crowded around on both sides of the road. They all admonished, “Why have you taken this path to die? You were quite happy following the path to hell. How foolish! How foolish you are, really!”
Kyáblákánta said, “Whether I am foolish or clever, this is my path.”
They then smiled and said, “When you have decided to take this as your path, then proceed, undaunted by the thorns and sharp stones that can cause you to stumble from time to time.”

On the way, Kyáblákánta noticed that some of them were singing bawdy songs, some were dancing lewd dances and some had started publicity centres for pornography. They all called out to Kyáblákánta, “Come Kyáblá, please come here and sit with us. Why the hell have you taken the path to heaven?”
Kyáblákánta said, “This path is my path.” He said,
Nindantu niitinipunáh yadi vá stuvantu,
Lakśmii samávishatu gacchtu vá yat́heśt́ham,
Adyeava marańamastu yugántare vá,
Nyáyát pathah praticalanti padaḿ na dhiiráh.

[Whether moral philosophers commend me or condemn me, whether Laksmi, the goddess of wealth, remains in the house or leaves the house in disgust on account of my walking, even if I die today on account of this journey or die after an infinite period of time, I shall never swerve from the path which I have taken as the right one. I shall not budge an inch.]
Prárabhyate na khalu bighna-bhayena niicaeh,
Prárabhya bignabihatáh viramanti madhyáh,
Bighnaermuhurmuhurapi pratihanyamánáh,
Prarabdhamuttamáh janáh na parityájanti.

“People of low calibre hesitate to take up any difficult work for fear of opposition; people of medium calibre start a difficult project but give up as soon as an obstacle comes, leaving it unfinished; and people of high calibre stick to the path that they have embraced as their own, despite obstacles at every step. All of you know what calibre of a person I was in the past. Now, if from today I want to become a person of high calibre, do you have any objection to it?”
They said, “No we donʼt have any objection. In fact, we were only testing you. Fare forward.”

After walking with great difficulty for six years, Kyáblákánta at last reached the gate of heaven. When he saw the person standing by the gate, he thought, “How strange! The person in charge of security here is none other than the angel who is my friend!”
The angel expressed his joy on seeing him. He was delighted. Kyáblákánta said, “My friend, now please allow me to enter heaven.”

The angel said, “I would also very much like you to come in, but the ledger recording the incidents of your life does not mention any good work you have done, on the strength of which you can enter heaven. Most of the figures are not written in black but in red.”
Kyáblákánta said, “But you are the supreme authority here. Canʼt you let me in because I am your friend?”
The angel said, “We have to abide by the rules. Any attempt to exercise special rights may be interpreted as nepotism.”
Kyáblákánta said, “But you can put in a word in my favour to Brahamá, Viśńu and Maheshvar.”

The angel said, “That will be of no use because Brahamá, Viśńu and Maheshvar always say that the exercise of discretionary power for somebody will always be seen as nepotism. So they never do it. You had better take several strolls between this gate and the junction where the three roads converge. By then, I will have straightened out your record and shall certainly allow you to come in.”

Very reluctantly, Kyáblákánta was about to go back when a thought came to him, “On what grounds should I keep the angelsʼ plastic bag with me when he follows every rule so religiously? Rather, let me return it to him.”
He told the angel, “My dear friend, I want to walk on this thorny path with free hands and feet. Please take your bag and keep it.”

The angel said, “I know and admit that a gifted article should not be taken back. But this time, I take the bag only to lighten your burden.” After saying this, he kept the bag within the precincts of heaven.
Suddenly, an idea struck Kyáblákánta. He remembered the magic quality of the bag. He looked about himself and said, “I wish that I go into that bag.”

Who could stop him then? He slowly entered the bag. The bag was within the premises of heaven. So now, Kyáblákánta was also within the premises of heaven. The angel was nonplussed. If the rules of entry into heaven are very strong, the rules of expelling somebody from heaven are still stronger. Humans go to heaven by dint of their own work. A new ledger card would now have to be prepared for recording the type of work that Kyáblákánta would do after his entry into heaven.
The angel said, “Well, my dear friend, since you have already arrived in heaven, let us build an ideal heaven together.”
Kyáblákánta resides in heaven to this day.

In Sanskrit, lap means to talk, to discuss, to speak with a dragging intonation. If you speak in a dragging manner, then the vocative case comes close to the nominative case. In the sentence, “Rama, what are you saying?” the word “Rama” is used in the vocative case. Again, if I say, “What is Rama saying?”, with a pause between “What is” and “Rama”, then “Rama” is used in the nominative case. In this connection, you must have heard of this well-known story.

There once lived a rich, old woman. The only descendant that she had from all her three family lines was her nephew, Harekrśńa. Harekrśńa was not a good man. Since he was going to inherit the huge property of his aunt after her death, he anxiously looked forward to the day when she would die. But his aunt was not dying at all. Harekrśńa became impatient. Some wicked people said that one night, he murdered his aunt. There was a police enquiry and lawsuits. Many villagers said that they had heard the old lady shouting at the top of her lungs, “I am being murdered! Oh, I am being murdered by Hare!”

In the normal course of events, the case would have been filed against Harekrśńa. Harekrśńa sought the help of a famous lawyer. The lawyer told the court, “Yes, of course, it is certainly true that at the time of her death, the old lady shouted, ‘Iʼm being murdered by Hare!ʼ Harekrśńa was the only relative of the old lady. Harekrśńa was her only hope and support. Those wicked villagers who had possibly heard the old lady shouting at the time of her death, ‘Iʼm being murdered by Hare!ʼ actually killed the old lady. In that situation, whom could the old lady call for help? She naturally called her nephew, her only support, and shouted, 'Hare ámáy márle!ʼ [Hare, Iʼm being murdered!] In other words, she wanted to say, 'Hare! Please come and see me, people are killing meʼ. She called ‘Hare’ only with the hope that Hare would come to her rescue. In this case, the old lady used the word ‘Hare’ not in the nominative case but in the vocative case.”

So you understand that according to the lawyer, the old lady uttered the word “Hare” in a long, dragging intonation. Since there was a little pause between the two words Hare and ámáy [me], people mistakenly thought that the old lady was saying that it was Hare who was trying to murder her. However, the lawyer, by distancing the word ámáy from Hare in articulation, convinced the judge of Hareʼs innocence.

I have an actual experience of hearing someone speak in a dragging intonation. I knew a gentleman whose name was Ramaranjan Roy. In normal conditions, he spoke in bursts with pauses in between, and in unnatural conditions, he spoke in a drawling intonation. It sounded like he was singing a classical song in normal conditions and a modern or film song in unnatural conditions. One evening, I was looking for Dharaniidhar Dhara, a very intimate acquaintance of mine, for some work. On the street I ran into Ramaranjan. Ramaranjan said, “Oh yes, just now I saw Dharaniidhar. I saw him under that shyáoŕá [ghost] tree.” He pronounced the words emphatically.
I dragged Ramaranjan towards the shyáoŕá tree. Evening was about to set. Indeed, Dharaniidhar and some of his friends were sitting under the shyáoŕá tree, enjoying the open air and chatting.

It was the time when the [evening] chiaroscuro of light and shade had just started playing through the crevices of the shyáoŕá tree. I had heard that ghosts were very fond of such an atmosphere and that was why they preferred the shyáoŕá tree to other trees. I said to Ramaranjan, “Look, what a ghostly atmosphere!”

Ramaranjan stuttered, “áṋ … áṋ … áṋ….” I noticed that he was unable to speak in bursts. We reached the shyáoŕá tree. Ramaranjan stood three steps behind me so that in case the ghosts suddenly came down from the tree, he would be the first person to run away.

I said, “Hello, Dharniidhar, I have been frantically looking (garu khoṋjá ( 1 )) for you for quite some time. Anyway, I didnʼt have to search long. Ramaranjan told me that you were sitting in seclusion under this shyáoŕá tree.”

Unfortunately, Ramaranjan was at that time haunted by the fear of ghosts. Terribly frightened, he said in a dragging intonation, “I didnʼt say that he was under the shyáoŕá tree. I said that he is near the shyáoŕá tree. Do humans ever stay under a shyáoŕá tree? Only the ‘gods’ (touching his forehead) that live in the shyáoŕá tree can rightfully sit under the shyáoŕá tree.”
Ramaranjan did not wait any longer.
Anyway, you now understand what is meant by speaking with a drawl.

We use the Sanskrit verbal root lup to mean breaking up. When we prepare a programme for a certain event, we divide the time into certain parts or periods. This kind of programme or breaking up of time is also called la. Intelligent human beings apply la to all their work. A good housewife, after lighting the stove, completes the tasks of cleaning the utensils, washing the rooms and other similar work. When the stove is ready, she will first boil the food that takes a long time to cook, then in the meantime she will complete other tasks such as cutting the vegetables, grinding the spices, taking her bath and worshipping. When there is a proper sense of la or organization, human life is fully enriched. Then the work done within oneʼs short, limited life assumes a rich significance, and the drama of life becomes a grand success. Otherwise, even a long life gets lost in darkness from sheer futility. Do you know the story of the weaving couple?

Once, there was a weaver and his wife. The wife never felt pressed for time in her housework. After firing the stove, she would do some weaving. After putting the rice pot on the stove, she would do some dyeing. After she had finished cooking and feeding her husband, she would go to the marketplace to sell some clothes, and on her way back she would buy groceries from the market. Not only did she do all the household chores, she wove and sold clothes as well. All the villagers were full of praise for her. And that was not all. Whenever anyone was in trouble, she would help them to the best of her ability. She could not afford to help financially but would give her own food instead. The villagers respected and loved her. They called her Vidyádharii.

The weaver was a man of just the opposite character. He would not sit up if he could remain lying down. He took one hour to chew the muŕi [parched-rice] that was his breakfast. During other meals, he would chew the dáṋtás [the stalk or stem of a plant] for one hour. After his lunch, he would smoke tobacco from a hubble bubble (gargaŕá) in a relaxed manner. He would scold his wife if there was any delay in preparing the tobacco. He would bring money to the market to purchase and smoke ganja without telling his wife.

One day, while he was returning from the market after consuming ganja, his fellow ganja smokers told him, “Dear weaver, you are an ideal person in our society. We request you to become the President of our Association of Ganja Consumers.” The weaver agreed to the proposal.

One day, at a meeting of the Ganja Consumers, this subject came up for discussion: “What is the fundamental truth of human life?” The members offered different answers. Some said, money; some said, paddy; some said, the plough and the bullock. No one could give the correct answer. In the Presidentʼs concluding speech, the weaver said, “The most useful thing on this earth is a pair of shoes.”
All the villagers asked, “Why? How so? How come?”

The weaver said, “What do we see in the shoes that we wear? In six months, the bottom of the shoes wears almost an inch down. Thatʼs why one has to repair the shoes or use new leather. Had we not used shoes, that wearing down would have taken place on our feet. In other words, our soles would have worn down an inch each in six months. This process of wearing down would have ultimately affected the entire body. That means there would have remained nothing like a body.”
The ganja addicts greatly admired the weaver.

One day, the weaver went out with his friends. As President, he walked in front. One of his friends put his foot in a well, mistaking it for the stairs to heaven, and was drowned. The other ganja addicts wondered, “What can be done now?”

The weaver said, “We must first understand the problem properly. Ask him. If he says he is dead, then send a message to his home. And if he does not give any reply, then we shall understand that he has reached home on his own.”
The ganja addicts were all full of praise for the weaver.

One evening, the police were out in search of ganja addicts. The weaver advised his friends who were ganja addicts, “Donʼt utter a single word as long as the police are around. They will know about your existence only if you speak.”

As President, he was the first to stand silently like a statue. The other ganja addicts, imitating him, also stood quietly in a line. Finding him standing in an unnatural manner, the police first asked the weaver, “Why are you standing like that?”
The weaver said, “How can I answer your question? I am only a lamp post and those who are standing by my side are palm trees.”
The ganja addicts were overwhelmed with admiration for the weaver. After the matter became public knowledge, the villagers named the weaver Bokendranáth [king of fools].
One day, one of the ganja addicts rushed to him and said, “Today, a strange thing happened! I heard a very strong rumour. It seems that the padmapukur [lotus tank] of the Pals is on fire!”
Borkendranáth asked, “Since the tank is on fire, what steps have the kai [anabas] fish taken to save themselves?”
The ganja addict replied, “Why should the kai fish worry? They quickly climbed up the palm tree.”

Brokendranáth protested in very strong language, “Thatʼs not possible. It is just not possible. It has never happened in the age of the Rámáyańa. It has never happened in the age of the Mahábhárata as well. How can it happen today? Which fool will believe that the kai fish climbed the palm tree? Are the kai fish cows that they will climb the palm tree?”

Vidyádharii was very much loved by all the villagers whereas the weaver was held in disrespect. Although they were of opposite natures, Vidyádharii and the weaver were very fond of each other. Vidyádharii did not like that people called the weaver Bokendranáth. At the slightest opportunity, she would praise the weaver before the villagers. And the weaver was always full of praise for Vidyádharii.

The days went by like this. But it became increasingly difficult to run the family. How long could Vidyádharii manage single-handedly? One day, she told Bokendranáth, “Look, you have a fine voice. You take some music lessons and then you will be able to make money by singing in the royal court.”
Bokendranáth said, “Learning music is no joking matter!”

Vidyádharii assured him, “If, while singing, you can beat time properly, everything will be easy. Here, I give you four rupees. Whatever comes to your view, sing about it and that will be your song complete with tune, rhythm and tempo.”
Bokendranáth said, “Suppose I take singing lessons. But to sing a song I also have to play the harmonium. Itʼs a very laborious job. I canʼt take so much strain.”
Vidyádharii said, “You will sing and I will play the harmonium.”
Bokendranáth said, “I have to go to the royal court and I have to sing a song when I reach there. The royal court is two miles away. I cannot walk so far.”
Vidyádharii said, “I will carry you on my shoulders.”

So Bokendranáth left his home in search of a music teacher. He was on the move but he did not know where to go. He did not know where to find a music expert. He only knew that a song originates in a particular collocation of sound. So, while walking. he kept his ears alert. Suddenly, he heard the very sweet, gentle sound of something falling quietly. After some searching, he found that an ant was digging a hole in a clay wall and the earth was slipping from that hole slowly and softly. Bokendranath realised that this was a song. He broke into song:
Jhur jhurá jhur mát́i paŕe,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[The earth glides down making a soft sound, Ták d́umád́um d́um.]

Since he had learnt the song from the ant, he threw a one-rupee coin to the ant. Behind him was Gadai Laskar (his real name was Gadadhar Laskar), brother of Madhai Laskar, an eminently rich man of that village, who was passing by and who had by chance witnessed this short scene. Gadai Laskar was astonished to see the activities of Bokendranáth. He picked up the coin and started following Bokendranath.

Bokendranáth continued walking. Suddenly, he noticed that he had trod on an earthworm (the synonym of keṋcho ( 1 ) is mahiilatá). The earthworm rolled up its body at once. When he saw this, Bokendranáth felt inspired and a song came gushing out like a fountain. He threw a one-rupee coin towards the earthworm and sang:
Bhaye gut́i shuṋt́i máre ták d́umád́um d́um.
[The earthworm curls up in fear
ták d́umád́umd́um.]

Bokendranáth moved on. He came near a kul ( 2 ) [jujube] tree. You certainly know that kuls and jáms [the rose apple] are the favourite food of jackals and foxes. At that time, a fox was sucking a jujube seed under a jujube tree. When it saw Bokendranáth, it left the place in fear and disgust. While fleeing, it looked back from time to time to see if Bokendranáth was chasing it. Again, the hot spring of song welled up in the heart of Bokendranáth. Fixing his eyes on the fox, he flung a one-rupee coin and broke into song:
Bhaye páláy ár pichu phire cáy re,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[It runs away in fear and looks behind from time to time,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.]

Gadai Lascar was very happy to pick up three rupees in succession and continued to follow Bokendranáth. Suddenly, Bokendranáth looked back. As he looked back, he noticed that Gadai Laskar, brother of Madhai Laskar, was standing there conspicuously. He broke into song:
Mádhái Laskarer bhái re,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[Oh, brother of Madhai Laskar,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.]
He threw a one-rupee coin towards Gadai Laskar and then bent down and respectfully touched his feet.

The day was drawing to an end. Bokendranáth returned home. When he reached home, he told his wife, “Vidyádharii, I have learned songs which will take the royal court by storm. But first give me something to eat. After that, I will sing the songs.”

With great gusto [komer beṋdhe, literally, tucking the saree into the waist to look smart], she began cooking. In one hour, she had cooked many items – biri kaláyer dál with hiḿ [blackgram pulse with asafoetida], maurii [fennel, aniseed] and mulá [radish] sliced into round pieces; posta [curry made with a paste of poppy seeds], kuler ambal [sour
broth made of jujube, a delicacy], diḿler ( 3 ) tarkári [curry made of red pumpkin] and ciṋŕer páyes [sweets made of milk and flat rice].

Bokendranáth ate the food with great relish. He ate up half the rice with láud́agá posta [curry made with a paste of poppy seeds and the tender upper end of the bottlegourd]. After his meal, while he was washing his hands, Vidyádharii quickly had her lunch. Then she sat at the harmonium. Just before singing, Bokendranáth, in the usual fashion of singers, said, “Today, I have some problem with my throat.”
Vidyádhariii hurriedly brought some hot ghee mixed with powdered black pepper and said, “Whenever your throat aches, you tell me. I will immediately pour one spoonful of hot ghee into your mouth.”

Bokendranáth began singing. Meanwhile, Gadai Laskar, brother of Madhai Laskar, was terribly perplexed. For so long, he had been under the impression that he was the richest man in the village and Bokendranáth was the poorest. But, today, what strange sights he had seen with his own eyes! Bokendranáth was carelessly throwing money away in the streets. He must have a huge amount of money at home stored in big, earthen containers.

It was the dead of night [nishuti: ni + shuti = nishuti, means when all have fallen asleep] when Gadai Laskar went with a burglarʼs tool and started cutting a hole in a comparatively soft part of the earthen wall of Bokendranáthʼs house. The earth started falling musically with the slightest stroke – jhur jhurá jhur, jhur jhurá jhur jhur jhurá jhur. Inside the house, Vidyádharii was playing on the harmonium and Bokendranáth was singing. He started with the song which he had learnt from the ants:
Jhur jhurá jhur mát́i paŕe,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[The earth glides down making a soft sound,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.]

After all, it was a classical song. So the same words had to be repeated umpteen times in different tunes. It is said that a maestro from Lucknow sang only four words for one hour – bajániyá cácániyá jhájhániyá, nácánayá – by singing them in different tunes. Similarly, Bokendranáth was repeating the same line in different tunes.

Gadai Laskar, engaged in cutting a hole, almost had a nervous breakdown when he heard the song. “Whatʼs happening?” he thought. “Could it be that Bokendranáth knows that the earth is gliding down melodiously because I am cutting the hole? Alas, I am undone!”

Gadai Laskar stopped cutting and quietly sat erect in the posture of kumbhak práńayáyam [physico-spiritual practice of controlling or suspending oneʼs breath] holding his breath. Vidyádharii then told Bokendranath, “Now begin the antará.”
Bokendranath began:
Bhaye gut́i shuṋt́i máre ták d́umád́um d́um.
[The earthworm curls up in fear
ták d́umád́um d́um.]

When he heard the antará, Gadai Laskar felt terribly frightened. He could feel his life ebbing away. He began to sweat all over with his bones crackling, head reeling and temple veins taut. Gadai Laskar remained sitting in that condition for some time more while Bokendranáth demonstrated his artistic skill in rendering the next antará:
Bhaye gut́i shuṋt́i máre ták d́umád́um d́um.
[The earthworm curls up in fear
ták d́umád́um d́um.]
Gadai Laskar realised that it was not safe for him to sit there for a long time. “Better that I flee now and look back from time to time to see if Bokendranáth is coming after me,” he thought.
Vidyádharii then told Bokendranáth, “Now start the next antará.” Bokendranath came to the next antará ( 4 ). He sang:
Bhaye páláy ár pichu phire cáy re,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[It runs away in fear and looks behind from time to time,
ták d́umád́um d́um.]

Gadai Laskar realised that the fact that he was fleeing and looking back from time to time to see if Bokendranáth was following him was also known to Bokendranáth. He wondered, “So what can be done? Can I be saved by fleeing?”
Inside the house, Vidyádharii told Bokendranáth, “Now, go back to ‘take’ [refrain],” Bokendranáth sang:
Mádhái Laskarer bhái re,
Ták d́umád́um d́um.
[Oh, brother of Madhai Laskar,
ták d́umád́um d́um.]

As soon as the words reached the ears of Gadai Laskar, his legs started shaking, his chest started heaving and his heart began throbbing violently. He thought, “Since I am caught, it will be more intelligent to surrender than to try to run away.” He remembered a song which he had once heard somewhere:
Viśva joŕá pháṋd petecho,
Kemane dii pháṋki,
Ádhek dhará paŕechi go,
Ádhek áche bákii.
[You have laid your trap all over the world,
How can I escape it?
I am already half caught,
And half is still left.]
Gadai Laskar said to himself that in his case, the song had to be slightly reworded. Lips shivering in fear, he now started singing:
Bokendranáth jál pheleche,
Kemane dii pháṋki,
Puro dhará paŕechi go,
Kichui náhi bákii.
[Brokendranath has cast his net,
How can I escape it?
I am fully apprehended,
Nothing is left.]
Gadai Laskar knocked at the door of Bokendranáthʼs house. He entered the house and broke down in tears. He blubbered, “I am extremely sorry. I have done something unlawful! Please pardon me.”

Vidyádharii realised that something very important must have happened in order for the fabulously rich Gadai Laskar to appeal so pitifully. So it was the time to exercise intelligence. Bokendranáth had not understood anything at all. He simply stared at Gadai Laskar like an idiot. As soon as Bokendranáth was about to ask, “What are you saying?” Vidyádharii interjected, “You! Why are you here? You … you … why are you here, go … go … go to the room … go to the room!” Saying this, she almost pushed Bokendranáth into the other room.

Vidyádharii had understood everything from Gadai Laskarʼs behaviour. She assumed a majestic posture and said sharply to Gadai Laskar, “Do you think I will let you off so easily? I am not exactly a fool. Just tell me what you want to say – speak in clear, unequivocal language.”

Vidyádharii understood everything that Gadai Laskar told her. After she had elicited all the information from Gadai Laskar, she said, “Such things cannot be settled so easily. There will be police cases, court cases. What do you think? You are a full moon! I will turn you into the moon of the dark night.”
Gadai Laskar said, “Please forgive me, madam, I prostrate before you. Please forgive me this time, at least.”
Vidyádharii replied, “If you want to be let off for all time, then pay me one lakh rupees in full. Then I shall see what can be done.”
Gadai Laskar counted one lakh rupees with his thumb with a rustling sound, performed expiatory exercises, obtained a pardon from Vidyádharii, and returned home.

After he left, Vidyádharii called Bokendranáth and related the entire story to him. Bokendranáth was dumbfounded. He said, “Vidyádharii, how intelligent you are, truly! To me, you are the visible adyáshakti [the primal power]. From now on, I shall religiously obey you. You have no match in the entire world.”

Vidyádharii said, “Stop this nonsense. Just listen to me and follow my words. Whenever you have to perform a job, divide the total time into several segments or la. After that, you draw up a schedule about which is to be done first and which later. Take into account all the pros and cons before you start any work. In case you have problems drawing up the schedule, just ask me and I shall advise you to the best of my intelligence. Do you understand!”

Bokendranáth quickly replied, “Yes I understand, I do understand, I thoroughly understand, I thoroughly understand. In every matter I shall turn to you for help, and look, I tell you, from today onwards, I shall touch your feet five hundred times every day.”

The gods from heaven started showering flowers on Vidyádharii. Bokendranáth called the attention of Vidyádharii, “Vidyedharii, have you observed the strange phenomenon that every flower is falling on your head and not a single one on mine?”
Vidyádharii said, “What does it matter? Donʼt worry about it; I shall pick up the flowers, make a garland from them and put it around your neck.”
Bokendranáth was beside himself with joy. The story of la ends here.
